subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Genesis 2: Creation of Man and Woman
question: Then the Lord God said, 'It is not good that the man should be alone;...'". Which term completes the divine declaration regarding the creation of a partner for man?
explanation: According to Genesis 2:18 (RSV), the Lord God said, 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him.'
proTip: Memorize exact phrasing from early Genesis narratives as examined in JAMB objective questions.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The first generation of mankind was destroyed in the great flood of water because of
explanation: Genesis 6:11-13 records that the earth was corrupt and filled with violence before God brought the great flood to destroy corrupt mankind.
proTip: Connect the ethical and moral decay described in pre-flood narratives with divine judgment.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Which of the following is the sign of the covenant between God and Abraham?
options: The sprinkling of blood on door posts
Circumcision in the flesh of the foreskins
explanation: According to Genesis 17:10-11, the physical sign of the everlasting covenant between God and Abraham's household was the circumcision of every male in the flesh of their foreskins.
proTip: Distinguish between the signs of different biblical covenants (e.g., rainbow for Noah, circumcision for Abraham, Sabbath for Moses).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: God appeared to Jacob in a dream and Jacob made a vow to
explanation: Following his dream at Bethel (Genesis 28:20-22), Jacob made a vow that if God would watch over him, the Lord would be his God, and of all that God gave him he would give a full tenth (tithe) to God.
proTip: Remember Jacob's vow at Bethel as an early biblical example of tithing and consecration.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Joseph and His Brothers in Egypt
question: Joseph saw his sale by his brothers as God's plan to enable him
explanation: When revealing himself to his brothers in Genesis 45:5-7, Joseph comforted them by stating that God sent him ahead of them to preserve life and save a great posterity.
proTip: Recognize the theological theme of divine providence overriding human wickedness in the Joseph narrative.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The two Hebrew midwives instructed by Pharaoh to kill the Hebrew male babies at birth were
explanation: Exodus 1:15 identifies the two God-fearing Hebrew midwives who defied Pharaoh's murderous orders as Shiphrah and Puah.
proTip: Commit the names of key minor figures in Exodus, such as the midwives, to memory.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The Egyptian magicians were able to reproduce the first three miracles done by Moses and Aaron, but the fourth which they were unable to perform was the plague of
explanation: According to Exodus 8:18-19, when Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod and struck the dust of the earth, there were gnats on man and beast; and the magicians tried to bring forth gnats by their secret arts, but could not.
proTip: Note the exact point where the Egyptian magicians acknowledged 'the finger of God' during the plagues.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Exodus: Crossing the Red Sea
question: The possibility of crossing the Red Sea was seen by Israel as
options: God's active presence in their midst
the miraculous power of Moses' rod
explanation: The miraculous deliverance through the Red Sea demonstrated God's mighty deliverance and active covenant presence safeguarding His people.
proTip: Understand the theological significance of the Exodus events as foundational acts of divine redemption.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: In Exodus 17 and Numbers 20, similar incidents of lack of water for the congregation are recorded. A significant difference however, is that in Exodus 17, Moses is commanded to
explanation: In Exodus 17:5-6, God instructed Moses to strike the rock at Rephidim to bring forth water, whereas in Numbers 20:8, he was commanded to speak to the rock.
proTip: Contrast the instructions in Exodus 17 (strike) with Numbers 20 (speak) to understand why Moses was later barred from entering Canaan.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Covenant and Law on Sinai
question: The only commandment which has a promise attached to it concerns
options: not taking the name of the Lord in vain
explanation: Exodus 20:12 details the fifth commandment ('Honour your father and your mother'), which explicitly includes the promise 'that your days may be long in the land which the Lord your God gives you.'
proTip: Remember that the fifth commandment is singled out by Paul in Ephesians as 'the first commandment with a promise'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" Who gave this riddle?
explanation: According to Judges 14:18, Samson propounded this famous riddle to his Philistine companions based on his encounter with the young lion and the bees' hive inside its carcass.
proTip: Associate famous biblical riddles and proverbs with their specific narrators and contexts.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Draw your sword and kill me, lest men say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" The speaker was
explanation: In Judges 9:54, when mortally wounded by a millstone dropped by a woman from the tower of Thebez, Abimelech desperately urged his armor-bearer to run him through so people would not say a woman killed him.
proTip: Pay attention to deathbed or dying speeches recorded in the historical books of Judges and Samuel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: A famous prophetess who was also a judge in Israel was
explanation: Judges 4:4 introduces Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, who judged Israel at that time and led them to victory alongside Barak.
proTip: Recognize key female leaders, judges, and prophetesses in the Old Testament.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Gideon was also called Jerubbaal because he
options: pulled down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it
led the Israelites against the Midianites who were Baal worshippers
turned Israel away from Baal worship
explanation: Judges 6:32 explains that Gideon was named Jerubbaal ('Let Baal contend against him') because he pulled down his father's altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah pole beside it.
proTip: Understand the etymology and historical background behind alternative names of biblical heroes.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom because
options: he did everything as the Lord had commanded him
Moses had laid his hand upon him
the Lord had promised to be with him as He was with Moses
he meditated on the book of the law day and night
explanation: Deuteronomy 34:9 records that Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, because Moses had laid his hands upon him; so the people of Israel obeyed him.
proTip: Note how leadership transfer and impartation of wisdom were historically authenticated in Israel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: My little finger is thicker than my father's loins" means that in comparison with his father, Rehoboam intended to
explanation: In 1 Kings 10 (or 12:10), King Rehoboam foolishly rejected the elders' advice and threatened the Israelites by boasting that his little finger would be thicker than his father Solomon's loins, meaning his rule would be significantly harsher and impose heavier forced labor.
proTip: Analyze royal metaphors used during political crises in the united and divided monarchies.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel!..." This declaration marked the end of
explanation: Recorded in 1 Kings 12:16, this rebellious declaration by the northern tribes led by Jeroboam marked the definitive split and end of the united kingdom of Israel.
proTip: Recognize the pivotal slogans and declarations that precipitated historical national schisms.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: The incident which inspired King Josiah to undertake a sweeping religious reform was the
options: discovery of the book of the law
explanation: According to 2 Kings 22, the discovery of the Book of the Law by Hilkiah the high priest during temple repairs deeply convicted King Josiah, inspiring his sweeping national religious reforms.
proTip: Connect King Josiah's religious revival directly to the finding of the lost scroll of the law.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice / True religion and Divine love: Amos
question: Seek good, and not evil, that you may live; and so the Lord, the God of hosts, will be with you, as you have said..." Which prophet gave this advice?
explanation: Amos 5:14 records this urgent prophetic call to righteousness, social justice, and repentance directed to the northern kingdom of Israel.
proTip: Associate ethical injunctions concerning social justice and equity with the prophet Amos.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: And at the time of the offering of the oblation, the prophet Elijah came near and said, 'O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel, and that I am thy servant, and that I have done all these things at thy word. Answer me, O Lord, answer me, that this people may know that thou, O Lord, art God, and that thou hast turned their hearts back.' What happened after this prayer?
options: The fire of the Lord fell
explanation: 1 Kings 18:37-38 records that immediately following Elijah's prayer on Mount Carmel, the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust.
proTip: Distinguish between the sequence of events on Mount Carmel (fire first, then rain).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Faith/Courage and Protection: Hezekiah and Isaiah
question: One of the reasons why Sennacherib could not enter Jerusalem and conquer it as he did to Samaria was that
options: his god told him to return home from his camp
thousands of his soldiers miraculously died overnight
he willingly changed his mind and returned to his country
fight broke out among his soldiers
explanation: According to 2 Kings 19:35, the angel of the Lord went forth and smote 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians, forcing Sennacherib to withdraw in defeat without conquering Jerusalem.
proTip: Remember the miraculous deliverance of Jerusalem under King Hezekiah through prophetic intervention.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: When the Chaldean army captured King Zedekiah, they
options: slew his wives before his eyes
cut off his fingers and toes
explanation: 2 Kings 25:7 details the tragic fate of King Zedekiah: they slaughtered his sons before his eyes, put out his eyes, bound him in bronze fetters, and took him to Babylon.
proTip: Note the specific cruelties inflicted during the final fall of Jerusalem and the capture of Zedekiah (note: option B is accurate regarding his sons/family in parallel accounts, but let's check standard textual specifics: they slew Zedekiah's sons before his eyes, and blinded him. subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all." This messianic prophecy was made by
explanation: This profound passage is found in Isaiah 53:6, part of the fourth Servant Song describing the vicarious suffering of the Messiah.
proTip: Memorize major messianic prophecies in Isaiah, especially chapters 7, 9, 11, and 53.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: The vision of 'dry bones' teaches that
options: there will be a resurrection of the body
there will be a new creation
explanation: In Ezekiel 37, the vision of the valley of dry bones is explicitly interpreted by God as representing the whole house of Israel in exile, symbolizing their national restoration and spiritual revival.
proTip: Distinguish between general apocalyptic resurrection theology and the specific historical/national application of Ezekiel's dry bones vision.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Gilgamesh Epic is the Babylonian equivalent of the biblical story of the
explanation: The ancient Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh contains a famous deluge account featuring Utnapishtim, serving as the ancient Near Eastern literary equivalent to the biblical flood narrative.
proTip: Be familiar with ancient Near Eastern parallels to early Genesis narratives.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Birth and Early Life of Jesus
question: To whom was the birth of Jesus announced with a sign?
explanation: In Luke 2:12, the angel announced the birth of Jesus to the shepherds, giving them a specific sign: 'You will find a babe wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.'
proTip: Note specific signs given during the infancy narratives in Luke's Gospel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The central message of John the Baptist in the Jordan region was about a baptism
explanation: The gospels consistently record that John went into all the region about the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
proTip: Distinguish between John's baptism of repentance versus Christian baptism in the Holy Spirit.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus heard a voice saying: 'Thou art my beloved Son; with thee I am well pleased.' Jesus heard this voice during His
explanation: This heavenly voice declared divine approval upon Jesus at His baptism by John in the River Jordan (Mark 1:11 and parallels).
proTip: Note that while similar words were spoken at the Transfiguration ('listen to him'), the exact phrase 'with thee I am well pleased' occurs at His baptism.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Herod, Jesus was John the Baptist raised from the dead because He
options: was a prophet like one of the prophets
had the powers of John at work in him
explanation: Frightened by reports of Jesus' miracles, superstitious King Herod exclaimed in Mark 6:14 that John the Baptist had been raised from the dead, which is why miraculous powers were at work in Him.
proTip: Understand the various public misconceptions concerning the identity of Jesus during His ministry.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: When John sent his disciples to ask Jesus 'Are you the one who is to come...?', Jesus' immediate reaction was to
options: ask them to tell John about his miracles
speak to the crowds concerning John
ask the crowds what they went into the wilderness to see
explanation: According to Luke 7:21, in that very hour Jesus cured many people of diseases, plagues, and evil spirits, and bestowed sight on many who were blind, before telling John's messengers to report what they had seen and heard.
proTip: Pay close attention to the precise sequence of actions in the gospels.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Birth and Early Life of Jesus
question: 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men with whom he is pleased!' is usually referred to as
explanation: This heavenly chorus sung by the multitude of the heavenly host praising God at the birth of Jesus in Luke 2:14 is traditionally known as the Angels' Song (Gloria in Excelsis Deo).
proTip: Identify well-known hymns and canticles embedded in the Gospel of Luke (e.g., Magnificat, Benedictus, Nunc Dimittis, Gloria).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith." This statement was made during the healing of the
explanation: Jesus expressed utter amazement and commended the extraordinary faith of the Roman centurion in Capernaum whose servant was healed from a distance (Luke 7:9 / Matthew 8:10).
proTip: Note instances where Jesus marveled at or commended Gentile faith over against Israelite unbelief.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: When they saw the man who had been possessed by demons in his right mind, the Gerasenes
options: asked Jesus to depart from them
asked Jesus to stay on with them
explanation: Following the destruction of the swine and the healing of the demoniac, the terrified people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes begged Jesus to leave their neighborhood (Mark 5:17).
proTip: Observe the negative economic and spiritual reaction of the townspeople to Jesus' powerful deliverance miracles.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: One of the objectives, according to Mark, for which Jesus appointed the twelve, was for them to
options: make disciples of all the nations of the earth
denounce the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and the Sadducees
explanation: According to Mark 3:14-15, Jesus appointed twelve to be with him, and to be sent out to preach and to have authority to cast out demons.
proTip: Pay attention to gospel-specific emphases regarding the appointment and commissioning of the twelve apostles.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Get behind me, Satan! For you are not on the side of God, but of men." The reason for this sharp rebuke was that the addressee
options: confessed that Jesus is the Christ
wanted to dissuade Jesus from dying on the cross
desired to be the right hand of Christ
explanation: Peter earned this severe rebuke immediately after his great confession because he took Jesus aside and rebuked Him for predicting His suffering and death, thereby setting his mind on human things rather than divine purposes (Mark 8:32-33).
proTip: Contrast Peter's flash of divine revelation with his human stumbling over the necessity of Christ's suffering.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: From the parable of the friend at midnight, we learn that
options: we should always make our requests even at midnight
we cannot receive anything from God if we don't ask
an evil father will always give good gifts to his children
the heavenly Father will always give the Holy Spirit to anybody who asks with persistence
explanation: In Luke 11:5-13, Jesus uses the parable of the importunate friend at midnight to teach persistence in prayer, concluding that the heavenly Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.
proTip: Relate the parable of the friend at midnight to themes of persistent prayer and divine generosity.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: And he was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan; and he was with the wild beasts; and the angels ministered to him. Jesus was led into the wilderness by
explanation: Mark 1:12 explicitly records that immediately after His baptism, 'the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.'
proTip: Note Mark's vivid use of the word 'driven' (ekballei) regarding the Spirit's prompting into the wilderness.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Which of the following instructions was given only to the seventy and not to the twelve when Jesus sent His disciples on missions?
options: Wipe off the dust from their feet
Salute no one on the road
explanation: In Luke 10:4, when sending out the seventy-two (seventy), Jesus gave the specific urgent instruction: 'carry no purse, no bag, no sandals; and salute no one on the road.'
proTip: Compare the specific instructions given to the twelve in Matthew 10 with those given to the seventy in Luke 10.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: But new wine must be put into fresh wine-skins." What issue was raised to which this statement was a response?
explanation: This teaching of Jesus regarding garments and wineskins (Mark 2:18-22) was given in direct response to questioning regarding why John's disciples and the Pharisees fasted, but Jesus' disciples did not.
proTip: Understand the theological transition from old religious rituals to new covenant realities through Jesus' parables.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's." The above quotation teaches
explanation: This famous teaching establishes Christian civic responsibility, commanding proper recognition of legitimate civil governance alongside absolute devotion to God.
proTip: Connect Jesus' statement on tribute money to New Testament ethics regarding civic duties.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Who requested the body of Jesus after His death?
explanation: All four gospels record that Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who was also looking for the kingdom of God, boldly asked Pilate for the body of Jesus and buried Him.
proTip: Remember that Joseph of Arimathea (assisted by Nicodemus) cared for the burial of Jesus.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road...?" This expresses the experience of
explanation: This statement was joyfully exclaimed by Cleopas and his companion after the resurrected Jesus vanished from their sight at Emmaus (Luke 24:32).
proTip: Associate the Emmaus road post-resurrection appearance with Cleopas and the breaking of bread.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Paul was accused of apparently being a preacher of foreign divinities in Athens because he preached Jesus and the
explanation: Acts 17:18 records that when Paul preached Jesus and the resurrection (Anastasis), the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers thought he was a preacher of foreign divinities.
proTip: Note how Greek philosophical skepticism encountered core Christian doctrines like bodily resurrection in Athens.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: When Paul and Barnabas healed a cripple at Lystra, the people named them
explanation: Acts 14:12 notes that the Lycaonian crowd called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul, because he was the chief speaker, they called Hermes.
proTip: Distinguish between Greek and Roman mythological counterparts (Zeus/Jupiter, Hermes/Mercury) mentioned in Acts.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Paul told the Athenians that they were very religious because
options: some of their poets said that men are the offspring of God
they dedicated an altar to the Unknown God
their Epicurean and Stoic philosophers always discussed religious issues
the city was full of idols and symbols of religious devotion
explanation: In Acts 17:22-23, Paul opened his address by noting that in every way they were very religious, having observed their sacred shrines and an altar inscribed 'To the unknown god.'
proTip: Analyze Paul's contextualized preaching strategy at the Areopagus in Athens.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The elders at Jerusalem advised Paul on his arrival in the city to
options: purify himself along with men under vows
join those in the temple for prayer and fasting
explanation: Acts 21:23-24 records that James and the elders advised Paul to join four men who had taken a vow, undergo purification rites with them, and pay their expenses to prove his fidelity to the Law.
proTip: Understand the cultural and legal compromises undertaken by early apostles to maintain peace among Jewish believers.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent; for I am with you, and no man shall attack you to harm you; for I have many people in this city." The city referred to was
explanation: According to Acts 18:9-10, the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision by night in Corinth, encouraging him not to be afraid because God had many people in that city.
proTip: Associate divine encouragements in visions with specific missionary stations in Acts.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: To the question of the Philippian jailer, 'Men, what must I do to be saved?' Paul replied,
options: Confess your sins and give alms
Release us and wash our wounds
Trust in God and pray always
explanation: Acts 16:30-31 records the direct and famous reply given by Paul and Silas: 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'
proTip: Memorize core evangelical conversion declarations recorded in the Acts of the Apostles.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Let it be known to you then that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen." This implies that
options: the Gentiles will be more receptive to Christianity than the Jews
the Jews have lost the opportunity of salvation forever
Paul has completely lost hope in the Jews
explanation: At the conclusion of his ministry in Rome (Acts 28:28), Paul declared this statement to emphasize that despite Jewish rejection in various quarters, the message of salvation finds open-hearted reception among Gentiles.
proTip: Trace the theological shift from Jewish rejection to Gentile inclusion throughout the Book of Acts.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: During the voyage to Rome, some people thought that Paul was a god because
options: he was not harmed by a viper
explanation: Acts 28:3-6 recounts how the native people of Malta expected Paul to swell up or fall dead after a venomous viper fastened on his hand, but when he suffered no harm, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
proTip: Note the miraculous signs accompanying Paul's shipwreck journey and arrival in Malta.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Be fruitful and multiply...". This statement occurs first in Genesis following the creation of
explanation: According to Genesis 1:22, the first time the divine command 'Befruitful and multiply' occurs is upon the creation of living creatures and birds (the aquatic creatures and birds on the fifth day), prior to its repetition for humans on the sixth day.
proTip: Pay attention to the exact order and repetition of divine blessings across creation days.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: ... Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for God made man in his own image...". The above passage explains the
explanation: In Genesis 9:6, God establishes the sanctity of human life because man is made in the image of God, underscoring the supreme theological importance and sacredness of blood and life.
proTip: Connect post-flood covenants with the foundational theological view of human dignity and life.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The four promises of God to Abram were land,
options: Many descendant, greatness and medium of blessings
explanation: In Genesis 12:1-3, the core covenant promises made to Abraham consist of land, numerous descendants, personal and national greatness, and becoming a medium/source of blessing to all families of the earth.
proTip: Memorize the components of the Abrahamic covenant as detailed in Genesis 12.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: God has made laughter for me; every-one who hears will laugh over me." This statement was made at the birth of
explanation: Genesis 21:6 records Sarah's joyful exclamation upon the birth of Isaac, noting that God had brought her laughter and that everyone who hears of it will laugh with her.
proTip: Associate the etymology and expressions of laughter with the miraculous birth of Isaac.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Joseph and His Brothers in Egypt
question: The main point emphasized in the story of Joseph's treatment of his brothers in Egypt was that
options: God's design for anybody cannot be stopped
it is good to forgive one's enemies
one should test any old enemy before trusting him
explanation: The overarching theological motif of the Joseph narrative demonstrates divine providence, showing that human wickedness cannot thwart God's sovereign purpose and design.
proTip: Recognize divine sovereignty as the primary theological takeaway from the Joseph cycle.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Put off your shoes from your feet; for the place where you stand is holy." Where was this statement made?
explanation: According to Exodus 3:5, God spoke these words to Moses from the burning bush at Mount Horeb (the mountain of God).
proTip: Distinguish between Mount Horeb (where Moses was called and received instructions at the burning bush) and Mount Sinai (where the Law was given).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Exodus: Crossing the Red Sea
question: When the Israelites were caught between Pharaoh's army and the Red Sea, God instructed Moses to
options: command the sea to be divided
throw his rod into the sea
stretch out his hand over the sea
explanation: Exodus 14:16 records that God explicitly commanded Moses to lift up his staff and stretch out his hand over the sea to divide it so the Israelites could go through on dry ground.
proTip: Note the exact physical action required of Moses during the parting of the Red Sea.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Who is the Lord that I should heed his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and moreover I will not let Israel go." How did Pharaoh react initially to this demand?
options: He appealed to them to stay in Egypt
explanation: Exodus 5:6-9 details how Pharaoh responded to Moses and Aaron's demand by increasing the burdens on the Hebrew slaves, stopping the supply of straw for making bricks.
proTip: Understand how initial confrontations between prophetic figures and oppressive rulers often escalate hardship before deliverance.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Which of the following is a condition for the eating of the Passover?
options: A fatted lamb should be taken from among the sheep or goat
Anything that remained until morning should be burnt
The lamb should be eaten boiled with its head, legs and inner parts
It should not be eaten in haste
explanation: According to Exodus 12:10, a specific instruction for the Passover meal was that nothing of it should remain until morning, and anything left over by morning must be burned with fire.
proTip: Review the ritual regulations governing the original Passover observance in Exodus 12.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Covenant and Law on Sinai
question: Before God met with Israel at Mount Sinai, Moses charged his people not to
options: tremble at the sight of smoke
tremble at the sound of thunder
explanation: Exodus 19:12 records that Moses set bounds around the mountain and charged the people, saying, 'Take heed that you do not go up into the mountain or touch the border of it; whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death.'
proTip: Note the holiness requirements and boundaries established around Mount Sinai during the covenant giving.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: It is not the sound of shouting for victory, or the sound of the cry of defeat, but the sound of singing that I hear." What occasion is reflected in this statement?
options: consecration of the Israelites at Mount Sinai
explanation: Exodus 32:17-18 records that when Moses and Joshua heard the noise from the camp during the golden calf incident, Moses declared it was neither shouting for war nor cries of defeat, but the sound of singing associated with idol worship.
proTip: Distinguish between the sounds heard during Israel's apostasy at Sinai and genuine military events.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: In order to stay alive, anyone who was bitten by the fiery serpent had to
explanation: Numbers 21:9 records that Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole; and if a serpent bit any man, when he looked at the bronze serpent, he lived.
proTip: Remember the looking at the bronze serpent as an Old Testament foreshadowing of faith in Christ (John 3:14).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: ... As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will not fail you or forsake you...". In the above passage, God addresses
explanation: According to Joshua 1:5, God gave this encouraging assurance of divine presence and leadership to Joshua as he prepared to lead Israel across the Jordan into the Promised Land.
proTip: Associate Joshua 1:5 with the commissioning and encouragement of Joshua after Moses' death.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The cities of the Amorites were completely devastated by Israel through the combined forces of
explanation: In biblical accounts of the conquest (such as Joshua 10 regarding the coalition of Amorite kings), divine intervention involved panic sent among the enemy, hailstones from heaven, and the sword of Israel.
proTip: Note the divine and human agencies cooperating in the conquest narratives of Joshua.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: In which of the Philistine cities did Samson carry away on his shoulder, the doors, posts and bar of the city gate?
explanation: Judges 16:2-3 records that when the citizens of Gaza locked their city gates to trap Samson overnight, he arose at midnight, lifted the doors of the gate along with the two posts and bar, put them on his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the hill that faces Hebron.
proTip: Memorize the specific feats of strength and locations associated with Samson's exploits in Judges.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice / True religion and Divine love: Amos
question: The king that reigned in Samaria during the prophecies of Amos and Hosea was
options: Jeroboam, the son of Joash (Jeroboam II)
explanation: Amos 1:1 and Hosea 1:1 state that their prophetic ministries occurred during the reign of Jeroboam the son of Joash (Jeroboam II), King of Israel.
proTip: Distinguish between Jeroboam I (who split the kingdom) and Jeroboam II (under whom Amos and Hosea prophesied).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Faith/Courage and Protection: Elijah and Elisha
question: The king who disguised himself when he traveled to Ramoth-gilead was
explanation: According to 1 Kings 22:30, King Ahab of Israel disguised himself and went into battle at Ramoth-gilead, though he was ultimately struck by a random arrow and died.
proTip: Remember Ahab's fatal disguise at Ramoth-gilead as prophesied by Micaiah.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Which of the following kings built the city of Samaria?
explanation: 1 Kings 16:24 records that King Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city on the hill, naming it Samaria after Shemer.
proTip: Attribute the founding and building of the capital city Samaria to King Omri.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice / True religion and Divine love: Amos
question: The theme of Amos's prophecies centres on the
explanation: The prophetic ministry of Amos is famously centered on moral righteousness and social justice (Amos 5:24: 'Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an everflowing stream').
proTip: Associate Amos distinctively with social justice and righteousness.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Punishment and Hope: Fall of Samaria
question: The event which ultimately led to the destruction and deportation of the Northern Kingdom was the invasion of
explanation: The Northern Kingdom of Israel fell to the Assyrian Empire under Shalmaneser and Sargon II in 722/721 B.C. due to persistent apostasy and covenant breaking.
proTip: Remember that Assyria conquered the Northern Kingdom (Samaria), while Babylon conquered the Southern Kingdom (Jerusalem).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Faith/Courage and Protection: Hezekiah and Isaiah
question: What was king Hezekiah's reaction to the letter of threat from the Assyrian king (Sennacherib)?
options: He spread it before God in the temple and prayed
He sent for his fellow kings to come and assist him
He summoned his soldiers to fight the Assyrians
He sent to the prophets for advice
explanation: According to 2 Kings 19:14-19, when Hezekiah received the threatening letter from Sennacherib, he went up to the house of the Lord, spread it before the Lord, and offered a heartfelt prayer for deliverance.
proTip: Associate King Hezekiah's exemplary faith during crises with his act of spreading letters of threat before God.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Manasseh did what was evil in the sight of the Lord because he
options: waged wars against the people of God
explanation: 2 Kings 21 details how King Manasseh undid his father Hezekiah's good work by rebuilding high places, erecting altars for Baal, making an Asherah pole, and worshiping all the host of heaven.
proTip: Remember Manasseh as the king in Judah most notoriously associated with extreme idolatry and pagan practices.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Who was the last king of Judah that suffered at the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon?
explanation: 2 Kings 25 records that Zedekiah was the final ruling king of Judah whose sons were killed before his eyes, after which he was blinded and taken in chains to Babylon.
proTip: Distinguish Zedekiah as the last blinded king of Judah from Jehoiachin who was exiled earlier.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: The image of jealousy which Ezekiel saw was the
options: worship of Baal in the land of Israel
explanation: In Ezekiel 8:3-5, the prophet is shown in a vision at the northern entrance of the altar gate of the temple, where the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy, was located.
proTip: Note the specific temple abominations and visions recorded by Ezekiel in chapters 8 through 10.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Concern for Judah / Return from Exile
question: What reason did the people around Jerusalem give for wanting to assist the returned exiles in rebuilding the temple?
options: They shared the same geographical location with the Jews
They themselves were Jews by descent
They were commanded to do so by king Cyrus of Persia
They also worshipped the same God as the Jews
explanation: According to Ezra 4:2, the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin approached Zerubbabel and the heads of families saying, 'Let us build with you; for we seek your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of King Esar-haddon of Assyria.'
proTip: Understand the socio-religious dynamics and conflicts during the rebuilding of the temple under Ezra and Nehemiah.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Jeremiah's vision of the rod of almond was meant to symbolize that God
options: would protect Jeremiah at all times
would confirm His word through Jeremiah
would send evil from the North upon the people
had appointed Jeremiah as a prophet before his birth
explanation: In Jeremiah 1:11-12, God shows Jeremiah a branch of an almond tree and explains: 'You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it' (using a Hebrew pun between *shaked* [almond] and *shoked* [watching]).
proTip: Connect Jeremiah's vision of the almond rod with God's vigilance in fulfilling His spoken word.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Birth and Early Life of Jesus
question: Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel....". This implies that
options: many Israelites would be saved (and others stumble)
explanation: Simeon's prophecy during the presentation of Jesus in the temple (Luke 2:34) indicates that Jesus' ministry would cause the falling (ruin) of unbelievers and the rising (salvation) of believers in Israel.
proTip: Understand Simeon's prophetic declarations in Luke 2 regarding the polarizing impact of Jesus' mission.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Birth and Early Life of Jesus
question: ... Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" Who asked Jesus this question or to whom was this said?
explanation: Jesus spoke these words in Luke 2:49 in response to His bewildered parents, Joseph and Mary, when they found Him debating with teachers in the temple at age twelve.
proTip: Associate Jesus' first recorded words in the Gospels with His exchange with Mary and Joseph in the temple.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: ... Rob no one by violence or by false accusation, and be content with your wages." To which group was this advice given by John the Baptist?
explanation: Luke 3:14 records that when soldiers asked John the Baptist what they should do, he instructed them not to extort money by violence or false accusation, and to be content with their wages.
proTip: Distinguish the specific behavioral demands John gave to soldiers versus tax collectors and the general crowd.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: ... The heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form, as a dove, and a voice came...". When did this occur?
explanation: Luke 3:21-22 explicitly records that while Jesus was praying after being baptized, heaven opened and the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in bodily form like a dove.
proTip: Connect the descent of the Holy Spirit like a dove directly to Jesus' baptism.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: James and John caused the other disciples of Jesus to be angry because they
options: did not go with the others on the missionary journey
asked for a special favour to sit with Jesus in glory
deflected to join the disciples of John the Baptist
explanation: Mark 10:41 (and Matthew 20:24) records that when the other ten disciples heard about the request made by James and John for seats of honor at Jesus' right and left hands in His glory, they became indignant.
proTip: Understand how ambition and status-seeking among the disciples generated friction in the apostolic community.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: What is the significance of Jesus allowing His disciples to take certain things and not others on their missionary journey?
options: Adequate material and spiritual preparation should be made for the work
He should depend on his audience for every need
He should have absolute confidence in the sufficiency and provision of God
He should not leave a place where he is not received without placing a curse
explanation: The strict travel instructions given to disciples (taking no extra money, bag, or spare tunics) were designed to teach them absolute dependence upon God's providential provision through hospitable receivers.
proTip: Grasp the theological rationale behind itinerant apostolic poverty and reliance on divine providence.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure..." What event does 'departure' refer to?
explanation: Luke 9:31 notes that Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and spoke of Jesus' 'departure' (*exodos*), which He was to accomplish at Jerusalem (referring to His suffering, crucifixion, and resurrection).
proTip: Note how Luke uses the term 'exodos' to describe Jesus' impending passion and death.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus pronounced 'woe' on the rich during the sermon on the plain because they
options: had received their consolation/reward in full on earth
explanation: In Luke 6:24 (Sermon on the Plain), Jesus declares, 'Woe to you that are rich, for you have received your consolation,' contrasting earthly wealth with eternal heavenly rewards.
proTip: Distinguish between Matthew's Beatitudes and Luke's paired Beatitudes and Woes on the Plain.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: In the parable of the sower, the seeds that fell on the rocky ground represent people who
options: believed for a short while and later fell away (due to no root)
believed and were later enticed by riches
were drawn away by worldly ambitions
explanation: Jesus explains in Luke 8:13 (and parallels) that the seed on the rock represents those who receive the word with joy when they hear it, but have no root; they believe for a while, but in time of testing fall away.
proTip: Master the four types of soil and their exact spiritual interpretations in the Parable of the Sower.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" How did Jesus respond to the rich ruler?
options: keep the commandments and surrender his wealth (sell all you have and follow me)
keep the commandments and pay tithe
do to others as he wished others to do to him
explanation: In response to the rich ruler (Luke 18:18-22), Jesus affirmed the commandments and then challenged him: 'Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor... and come, follow me.'
proTip: Understand the radical call to detachment from wealth in the encounter with the rich young ruler.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Go your way; your faith has made you well." This statement was addressed to
options: the woman with the issue of blood
explanation: In Mark 10:52 (and Luke 18:42), upon healing blind Bartimaeus outside Jericho, Jesus tells him, 'Go your way; your faith has made you well,' whereupon he immediately recovered his sight and followed Jesus.
proTip: Note how Jesus frequently attributes miraculous healing to the personal faith of the recipient.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The disciples could not cast out the dumb spirit from the epileptic boy because
options: they were not familiar with that particular spirit
it could only be driven out by prayer (and lack of faith)
explanation: Mark 9:29 records that when the disciples asked Jesus why they could not cast it out, He replied, 'This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer [and fasting].'
proTip: Connect spiritual authority in deliverance ministries with persistent prayer and spiritual discipline.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Which of the following groups did NOT believe in the resurrection of the dead?
explanation: The Sadducees were a prominent Jewish religious party during the time of Jesus who strictly rejected the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead, angels, and spirits (Acts 23:8).
proTip: Remember the theological differences between Pharisees (who believed in resurrection) and Sadducees (who did not).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The Holy Week starts with the
explanation: In Christian tradition and liturgical chronology, Holy Week commences with Palm Sunday, commemorating Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem.
proTip: Trace the chronology of events leading from Palm Sunday to the crucifixion during Passion Week.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Where did Jesus go after His triumphal entry into Jerusalem according to several accounts (like Mark 11:11)?
explanation: Mark 11:11 records that after entering Jerusalem and looking around at everything in the temple, because it was already late, Jesus went out to Bethany with the twelve.
proTip: Note the movements of Jesus between Jerusalem and Bethany during Passion Week.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Pilate delivered Jesus to be crucified because he
options: was afraid of the chief priests
explanation: Mark 15:15 explicitly records that Pontius Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd (and fearing a riot), released Barabbas for them and delivered Jesus, after scourging Him, to be crucified.
proTip: Identify political appeasement of the mob as Pilate's primary motive in condemning Jesus.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The two disciples on the way to Emmaus recognized Jesus
options: while He was teaching along the road
before they got to the village
at the breaking of bread while at table
explanation: Luke 24:30-31 recounts that as Jesus sat at table with Cleopas and his companion at Emmaus, He took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them—whereupon their eyes were opened and they recognized Him.
proTip: Associate the Emmaus road revelation of the risen Christ specifically with the breaking of bread.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Then after fasting and praying, they laid their hands on them and sent them off." What is the significance of the laying on of the hands in this passage (Acts 13:3)?
options: the Church under the guidance of the Holy Spirit commissioned and initiated the missionary work of Paul and Barnabas
the teachers' and prophets' hands conferred inherent divine authority on Paul and Barnabas
Paul and Barnabas were here ordained Levitical priests
Paul and Barnabas were confirmed as the first Christian Apostles
explanation: The laying on of hands by the prophets and teachers at Antioch signified the church's corporate commissioning and sending forth of Paul and Barnabas under the direct promptings of the Holy Spirit for their first missionary journey.
proTip: Understand the ecclesiastical significance of laying on of hands in the Book of Acts for missionary commissioning.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Mission to the Gentiles / Jerusalem Council
question: The reason for the first Apostolic Council in Jerusalem (Acts 15) was that
options: Paul's apostleship was violently disputed by local elders
circumcision and adherence to the Mosaic law were enjoined on Gentile converts as necessary for salvation
Gentiles were discriminated against at daily fellowship meals
widows of Hellenistic Jews were neglected in daily distributions
explanation: Acts 15:1-5 records that certain men came down from Judea teaching the believers, 'Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved,' sparking the Jerusalem Council.
proTip: Identify the Judaizing controversy over circumcision as the catalyst for the Jerusalem Council.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Before the Areopagus in Athens, Paul declared that the Unknown God was
options: indeed the Creator of the world and everything in it
a manifestation of the human psychological mind
explanation: Acts 17:24-25 records Paul's proclamation to the Athenians that the God whom they worshiped as unknown is the Creator of the world and all things in it, who does not dwell in shrines made by human hands.
proTip: Master Paul's apologetic approach at the Areopagus connecting Greek altar inscriptions to the Creator God.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Owing to the uproar in Jerusalem, the Roman tribune ordered Paul to be examined by scourging, but changed his mind when he discovered that Paul was
explanation: Acts 22:25-29 details how, as the soldiers bound Paul for scourging, Paul informed the centurion that he was a Roman citizen born free, causing the tribune to immediately halt the interrogation out of fear of violating Roman law.
proTip: Note how Paul's Roman citizenship frequently protected him from illegal abuse and granted him appeals to Caesar.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: When Paul and his companions were shipwrecked, the soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none would swim away and escape, but the centurion prevented them because
options: he would have to account for their lives with his own life
he wanted to save Paul's life specifically
it was against Roman military law to kill prisoners at sea
explanation: Acts 27:42-43 notes that while the soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners, the centurion Julius, wishing to save Paul, put a stop to their plan and commanded that those who could swim should jump overboard first.
proTip: Recognize divine providence operating through the centurion's personal regard for Paul during the shipwreck journey.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: ... You shall indeed hear but never understand, and you shall indeed see but never perceive..." To which prophet did Paul attribute this saying at the close of Acts (Acts 28:25-26)?
explanation: At the end of Acts 28, when quoting this passage regarding stubborn spiritual blindness among unyielding listeners, Paul attributes the saying to the prophet Isaiah.
proTip: Associate this famous prophetic judgment quote (Isaiah 6:9-10) with both Jesus' parables and Paul's final address in Rome.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: On arrival in Rome as a prisoner, whom did Paul address first according to Acts 28:17?
options: the local leaders of the Jews residing in Rome
explanation: Acts 28:17 records that three days after arriving in Rome, Paul called together the local leaders of the Jews to explain his situation and preach the gospel before turning fully to Gentiles.
proTip: Note Paul's consistent missionary pattern in Acts of preaching 'to the Jew first and also to the Greek.'

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Fall of Man and its Consequences (Genesis 3)
question: I heard the sound of thee in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself. The question that immediately followed this statement was...
options: What is this that you have done?
Who told you that you that you are naked?
Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?
explanation: According to Genesis 3:9-11, after Adam hid himself because he was naked, God's immediate question to him was, 'Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?' However, looking specifically at the exact sequence of questions posed in Genesis 3:11 following his excuse of hiding, God asks, 'Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?' Tracing the text verbatim: God first calls 'Where are you?' (v. 9), Adam responds about being naked and hiding (v. 10), and God immediately follows with 'Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?' Option 1 corresponds to 'Who told you that you are naked?'.
proTip: Pay close attention to the chronological dialogue order in Genesis 3 when dealing with the Fall narrative questions.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Flood and God's Covenant with Noah (Genesis 6–9)
question: One of the rules given to Noah after the flood was that he should
options: not to eat the flesh with its blood
explanation: In Genesis 9:4, as part of the covenant stipulations given to Noah and his sons after the flood, God explicitly commanded them: 'Only you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood.'
proTip: The dietary laws given to Noah emphasize the sanctity of life symbolized by blood, which reappears throughout biblical covenant traditions.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
question: ... Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you..." This statement was made by
explanation: In Genesis 27:29, Isaac pronounced this blessing upon his son Jacob (mistakenly thinking he was Esau), conferring supremacy and leadership over other peoples and his brethren.
proTip: Familiarize yourself with the patriarchal blessings given by Isaac to Jacob and Esau in Genesis 27.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Joseph in Egypt and the Preservation of Israel
question: This lad is gone; and where shall I go?" Which of Joseph's brothers uttered these words?
explanation: In Genesis 37:29-30, when Reuben returned to the pit and found that Joseph was missing, he rent his clothes and cried out, 'The lad is gone; and I, where shall I go?'
proTip: Know the distinct reactions of Joseph's brothers (especially Reuben and Judah) during the crisis of selling and losing Joseph.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Divine Providence/Guidance/Protection: Moses and the Exodus
question: Pharaoh oppressed the Israelites because
options: he feared that they might join his enemies to fight him
they continued to give birth to male children
the midwives did not kill the children at birth
he did not know Jacob and Joseph
explanation: According to Exodus 1:9-10, the new king of Egypt stated that the Israelites were too many and mighty, fearing that in the event of war, they would join their enemies and fight against Egypt, hence the decision to oppress them.
proTip: Understand the socio-political motives behind the Egyptian oppression of the Hebrews at the beginning of Exodus.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Divine Providence/Guidance/Protection: Crossing the Red Sea
question: ... The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be still..." The Lord fought for the people of Israel on the occasion referred to in the statement by
options: drowning the Egyptian army in the Red Sea
opening a chasm in the earth and swallowing their enemies
raining fire and brimstone on their enemies
raining hail and stones on their enemies
explanation: In Exodus 14:14, Moses spoke these words of assurance to the Israelites just before God parted the Red Sea and subsequently drowned the pursuing Egyptian army.
proTip: Connect key catchphrases like 'The Lord will fight for you' to the specific deliverance at the Red Sea.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Obedience and Disobedience: The Golden Calf
question: When Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the Israelites
options: decided to go back to Egypt
went up to look for him
asked Aaron to make gods for them
explanation: According to Exodus 32:1, when the people saw that Moses delayed coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron and demanded, 'Up, make us gods, who shall go before us...'
proTip: Note how human impatience in spiritual leadership often leads to moral and religious deviation, as seen in the Golden Calf incident.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Moses could not enter the promised Land because he
options: was too old to cross the border
was too busy preparing his successor
did not give due regard to God
explanation: According to Numbers 20:12 and Deuteronomy 32:51, Moses was barred from entering the Promised Land because he failed to uphold God's holiness and honor before the people at the waters of Meribah.
proTip: Leaders are held to strict standards of obedience; Moses' minor deviation at the rock cost him entry into Canaan.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Moses consecrated Joshua as the new leader of Israel in the presence of
explanation: According to Numbers 27:18-23, Moses consecrated Joshua before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation, laying his hands upon him as commanded by God.
proTip: Remember that after Aaron died, his son Eleazar succeeded him as high priest and stood alongside Joshua during leadership transitions.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you.." This pledge was made to Joshua by the
options: Reubenites, the Gadites and part of the tribe Manasseh
explanation: In Joshua 1:16-18, the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh pledged their total loyalty and obedience to Joshua, echoing the commitment made to Moses.
proTip: Pay attention to tribal commitments in the conquest narratives; the trans-Jordan tribes were the first to pledge full support to Joshua.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Conquest and Settlement: Rahab and Jericho
question: Rahab the harlot assisted the Israelites spies as they prepared to attack
options: the five kings of the Amorites
explanation: According to Joshua 2:1-6, Rahab hid the two spies sent by Joshua in her house in Jericho, protecting them from the king's search party.
proTip: Rahab's faith and actions in saving the spies at Jericho earned her a place in the genealogy of faith (Hebrews 11).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." This riddle was explained first to Samson's
explanation: According to Judges 14:16-17, Samson's wife (the woman from Timnah) wept over him and coaxed him until he explained the riddle to her, and she then revealed it to the Philistines.
proTip: Note the recurring theme in Samson's narrative where domestic pressure and marital betrayal compromise his secrets.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: For offending God, the Israelites were delivered into the power of Midian for
explanation: According to Judges 6:1, the Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord gave them into the hand of Midian for seven years.
proTip: Memorize the cycle of oppression and deliverance durations in the Book of Judges (e.g., Midianite oppression lasted 7 years).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Gideon was able to defeat the Midianites with a reduced number of soldiers because he
explanation: According to Judges 7, God deliberately reduced Gideon's army to 300 men so that Israel would not claim their own strength won the victory, anchoring their triumph purely on trust and faith in God's deliverance.
proTip: Divine victories in the Old Testament consistently emphasize reliance on God rather than human military might.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Elkannah would give Hannah only one portion of the sacrifice because
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 1:5, although Elkanah loved Hannah deeply, he gave her only one portion because the Lord had closed her womb, whereas Peninnah had children.
proTip: Understand the background of Samuel's birth and Hannah's sorrow at Shiloh due to childlessness.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
question: Who was unfaithful to her husband as Israel was to God?
explanation: According to Hosea 1:2-3, Gomer, the wife of Hosea, was unfaithful to him, acting as a living symbol of Israel's spiritual harlotry and unfaithfulness to God.
proTip: Gomer's unfaithfulness and Hosea's unconditional love mirror God's covenant relationship with wayward Israel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
subTopic: The Division of the Kingdom: Rehoboam and Jeroboam
question: ... To your tents O Israel!" This was a signal for
explanation: According to 1 Kings 12:16, when the northern tribes realized Rehoboam would not lighten their yoke, they shouted, 'What portion have we in David? ... To your tents, O Israel!', signaling total rebellion and the division of the kingdom.
proTip: Recognize this famous rallying cry as the definitive marker of the split of the United Monarchy.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
subTopic: Elijah and the Supremacy of God
question: As the Lord God of Israel lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain those years except by my words." Who was the Israelites king during the period of the drought?
explanation: According to 1 Kings 16:29 and 17:1, Ahab was the wicked king of Israel during whose reign Elijah declared the severe drought.
proTip: Match prophetic figures with their contemporary monarchs; Elijah confronted Ahab and Jezebel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
question: When Elishah received the message about Benhadad's ill-health, the prophet wept because
options: Benhadad would not recover from the sickness
Hazael would be cruel to Israel
explanation: According to 2 Kings 8:11-12, Elisha fixed his gaze and wept because he foresaw the immense cruelty and destruction that Hazael would inflict upon the people of Israel once he became king of Syria.
proTip: Elisha's tears over Hazael highlight the prophetic burden of foreseeing national tragedies.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
subTopic: Faith/Courage and Protection: Hezekiah and Sennacherib
question: ... Incline thy ear, O Lord, and hear, open thy eyes, O Lord, and see; and hear the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God..."This was the prayer of
explanation: According to 2 Kings 19:15-16, King Hezekiah spread the blasphemous letter from Assyrian King Sennacherib before the Lord in the temple and offered this earnest prayer for deliverance.
proTip: Hezekiah's response to crisis is a classic biblical model of turning to God in prayer during national threats.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
subTopic: Religious Reforms and Punishment in Judah: Manasseh's Sins
question: ...Behold, I am bringing upon Jerusalem and Judah such evil that the ears of every one who hears of it will tingle ..." The above was said because of the sins of
explanation: According to 2 Kings 21:11-12, because of the extreme wickedness and idolatry introduced by King Manasseh, God pronounced devastating judgment that would make ears tingle.
proTip: Manasseh's egregious idolatry and shedding of innocent blood sealed the doom of Jerusalem despite later reforms.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: David and Saul: Rise of David
question: Saul initially desired to kill David because
options: David became very popular after killing Goliath
David married Michal and befriended Jonathan
Saul was tormented by an evil spirit
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 18:7-9, Saul grew intensely jealous and suspicious of David after the women chanted that Saul had slain his thousands and David his ten thousands, sparking Saul's murderous intent.
proTip: Envy over public acclaim and popularity was the root cause of Saul's persecution of David.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: God revealed to Solomon that the kingdom would be divided after him because he
explanation: According to 1 Kings 11:9-11, God was angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from the Lord to worship foreign idols, leading to the divine decree that the kingdom would be torn from his son.
proTip: Idolatry and disobedience are primary catalysts for political judgment in Israelite history.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
subTopic: Holiness and Divine Call: Isaiah's Call
question: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and His train filled the temple." Which prophet is associated with this vision?
explanation: According to Isaiah 6:1, this glorious inaugural vision in the temple took place in the year King Uzziah died, calling Isaiah into prophetic ministry.
proTip: Always link Isaiah's prophetic call and vision of holiness to the death of King Uzziah.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: King Herod granted the request of the daughter of Herodias by beheading John the Baptist because
options: the King was impressed by the way she danced
John the Baptist opposed the king's love affairs with Herodias
Herod was bound by oath and personal integrity
Herod was anxious to see John the Baptist dead
explanation: According to Matthew 14:9 and Mark 6:26, although the king was grieved, because of his oath and the guests at his table, he commanded it to be given, valuing his public oath above life.
proTip: Foolish oaths driven by pride can lead to tragic moral compromises, as seen in Herod's execution of John.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Which of the following is NOT a condition for being a disciple of Jesus?
options: Having a good knowledge of the scriptures
Taking up of the cross daily
explanation: According to Jesus' teachings on discipleship (e.g., Luke 9:23, Matthew 10:32), self-denial, taking up one's cross daily, and confessing Christ before men are explicit requirements. Academic scriptural knowledge is not listed as a prerequisite condition for discipleship.
proTip: Discipleship in the Gospels is framed around surrender, obedience, and following Christ rather than formal scholarship.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Mark's Gospel, the first miracle of Jesus was
options: opening the eyes of a blind man
healing a man with an unclean spirit
raising a dead boy to life
explanation: According to Mark's Gospel (Mark 1:21-27), the very first public miracle performed by Jesus in the synagogue at Capernaum was casting out an unclean spirit from a possessed man.
proTip: Note that while John's Gospel records turning water to wine as Jesus' first sign, Mark's Gospel begins Jesus' public miracles with the healing of the demoniac in Capernaum.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: When the disciples thought that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately, Jesus told them the parable of the
explanation: According to Luke 19:11-27, because Jesus was near Jerusalem and the people supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately, He proceeded to tell the parable of the pounds (minas) to teach about delayed return and accountability.
proTip: Link the parable of the pounds in Luke 19 directly to correcting the misconception of an immediate earthly kingdom establishment.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The miracle which Jesus performed on the Sabbath was the healing of the
explanation: According to Mark 3:1-6 (and parallel synoptic accounts), Jesus healed the man with a withered hand in the synagogue on the Sabbath, sparking intense controversy with the religious leaders.
proTip: Sabbath healing controversies in the Gospels highlight Jesus' teaching that doing good and saving life supersede rigid legalism.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Sermon on the Mount / Plain: Beatitudes
question: Peace makers are blessed because they shall
options: be called the sons of God
explanation: According to Matthew 5:9, in the Beatitudes, Jesus pronounces: 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.'
proTip: Memorize the specific rewards attached to each Beatitude in Matthew 5 to avoid mixing them up.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me, ..." The above statement was addressed to
options: the 12 whom he sent out to preach
all the disciples, just before the Ascension
the 70 whom he sent out to preach
all the disciples during the Sermon on the Mount
explanation: According to Luke 10:16, Jesus addressed this vital principle of representation to the seventy disciples whom He sent out ahead of Him on mission.
proTip: Note that while similar authority statements are given to the twelve, Luke explicitly attributes this phrasing to the commissioning of the seventy.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
