subTopic: Miracles of Jesus: Raising the Dead
question: A great Prophet has arisen among us! and God had visited his people. "These statements were made during the
options: raising of the son of the widow of Nain
explanation: According to Luke 7:11-16, when Jesus raised the only son of the widow of Nain, fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, 'A great prophet has arisen among us!' and 'God has visited his people!'
proTip: Connect this exact proclamation of awe ('God has visited his people') to the raising of the widow's son at Nain in Luke 7.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus gave the sign of Jonah to the Pharisees to indicate his
options: three-fold office as Prophet, Priest and King
explanation: According to Matthew 12:39-40, Jesus explained that just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, so would the Son of Man be three days and nights in the heart of the earth, prefiguring His death and resurrection.
proTip: The 'sign of Jonah' is a direct prophetic metaphor used by Jesus for His upcoming burial and resurrection.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The Jews asked Jesus whether they should pay their tax or not because they wanted to
options: help him and his disciples to pay taxes
explanation: According to Matthew 22:15-18 and Mark 12:13, the Pharisees and Herodians sent their disciples to ask about paying taxes to Caesar specifically to entangle Him in His talk so they could accuse Him.
proTip: Recognize that trick questions in the Gospels were rarely born of genuine curiosity; they were traps set by religious authorities.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus began to teach his disciples about his suffering, rejection, crucifixion and resurrection after
options: the healing of the blind Bartimaeus
explanation: According to Mark 8:29-31 (and parallel synoptic accounts), immediately following Peter's great confession ('You are the Christ'), Jesus began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be killed.
proTip: Peter's confession marks the turning point in the Gospels where Jesus openly introduces the necessity of His suffering.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: ... For the Son of man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." This statement was made by Jesus
options: after healing two blind men near Jericho
immediately before he told the parable of the householder
during the discussion that followed the request of the sons of Zebedee
as he was foretelling his crucifixion and resurrection
explanation: According to Mark 10:35-45 and Matthew 20:20-28, this pivotal teaching on servant leadership and ransom was given right after the ambitious request by James and John (the sons of Zebedee) and the ensuing indignation of the other disciples.
proTip: Tie Jesus' definition of true greatness and service directly to the dispute sparked by the sons of Zebedee.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Herod was very glad to see Jesus at the trial because
options: John the Baptist spoke to him about Jesus
he believed that Jesus was the Messiah
he hoped to see Jesus perform some miracles
the quarrel between Herod and Pilate was settled on account of Jesus
explanation: According to Luke 23:8, when Herod saw Jesus he was very glad, for he had long desired to see Him because he had heard about Him, and he hoped to see some sign or miracle done by Him.
proTip: Herod viewed Jesus as a spectacle rather than a Savior, seeking miraculous entertainment during the trial.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!" This verse is connected with
options: the song of the disciples after the Last Supper
explanation: According to Luke 19:38, these exact words were shouted by the whole multitude of the disciples as praise during Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem.
proTip: Compare the angelic birth hymn in Luke 2 ('Glory to God in the highest...') with the triumphal entry acclamation in Luke 19 ('Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!').

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Mark, the people who saw where Jesus was laid were Mary Magdalene and
explanation: According to Mark 15:47, Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses (or James) saw where He was laid.
proTip: Pay close attention to gospel-specific details regarding who witnessed the burial and visited the tomb on resurrection morning.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The message of the risen Christ to the woman who came early to the tomb was to be relayed to the disciples and to
explanation: According to Mark 16:7, the angel instructed the women: 'Go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee...'—specifically singling out Peter.
proTip: The specific inclusion of Peter in the resurrection message signifies restoration after his threefold denial.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Fellowship in the Early Church: Healing the Lame Man
question: I have no silver and gold, but I give you what I have; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk." This was said by Peter to a lame man
explanation: According to Acts 3:2-6, Peter spoke these words to the beggar who was lame from birth while entering the temple at the gate called Beautiful.
proTip: Connect Peter and John's miraculous healing of the beggar directly to the temple gate called Beautiful in Acts 3.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Opposition to the Gospel: Martyrdom of Stephen
question: The immediate cause of the stoning of Stephen was his
options: declaration of Jesus as the Righteous One
condemnation of the Jewish rite of circumcision
claiming to see Jesus at the right hand of God
explanation: According to Acts 7:54-56, when Stephen declared, 'Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing at the right hand of God,' the crowd cried out, covered their ears, and rushed upon him to stone him.
proTip: Stephen's vision of the exalted Christ provoked the final fury of the Sanhedrin leading to his martyrdom.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Mission to the Gentiles / Paul's Journeys
question: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all with one voice cried out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" Who was the Jew alluded to here?
explanation: According to Acts 19:34, during the riot in Ephesus, when the crowd recognized that Alexander (or Gaius, depending on context in the riot where Jews pushed Alexander forward, but looking at the options: the crowd quieted when they realized someone was Jewish, or shouted against the Christians—let's verify Acts 19:33-34 where Alexander was put forward by the Jews, but the crowd shouted because they knew he was a Jew). Wait, let's examine Acts 19:33-34: 'And they pushed Alexander forward... and shouting for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"' Alexander was a Jew put forward to make a defense.
proTip: Review the Ephesian riot in Acts 19 involving Demetrius the silversmith and the defense offered by Alexander.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Mission to the Gentiles / Antioch Church
question: Saul and Barnabas were sent on their mission by the
explanation: According to Acts 13:1-3, after fasting and praying, the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch laid hands on Saul and Barnabas and sent them off on their first missionary journey.
proTip: The Antioch church served as the primary launching pad for Gentile missions rather than the Jerusalem church.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The Jerusalem Council sent a group of four, with a letter to Antioch. At the end of their mission, which of the following remained behind in Antioch?
explanation: According to Acts 15:22-33, Judas (called Barsabbas) and Silas were sent back with Paul and Barnabas. While Judas returned to Jerusalem, Silas chose to remain behind in Antioch to strengthen the brethren.
proTip: Silas's decision to remain in Antioch paved the way for his later partnership with Paul on the second missionary journey.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Opposition to the Gospel: Paul in Philippi
question: They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now cast us out secretly?..." This experience of Paul was in
explanation: According to Acts 16:37, Paul spoke these words to the magistrates of Philippi after he and Silas were publicly beaten and imprisoned without trial despite being Roman citizens.
proTip: Philippi was the site where Paul invoked his Roman citizenship rights following unjust imprisonment.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Paul's Return to Jerusalem and Vows
question: Paul purified himself in the Temple after the third missionary journey because he was
options: advised to do so by the elders
explanation: According to Acts 21:23-26, the elders in Jerusalem advised Paul to join four men who had a vow upon themselves, purify himself with them, and pay their expenses so that all would know there was no truth to rumors that he abandoned the Mosaic law.
proTip: Paul's participation in temple purification rituals demonstrates his cultural accommodation to ease Jewish-Christian tensions.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: During Paul's trial by the Tribunal, he brought a division between the Pharisees and Sadducees by mentioning the issue of
explanation: According to Acts 23:6-8, knowing that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, Paul cried out in the council, 'Brethren, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead I am on trial.' This immediately divided the assembly.
proTip: Paul cleverly utilized theological divisions between Pharisees and Sadducees (the resurrection doctrine) to disrupt his prosecutors.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: On the Island of Malta, Paul healed a man who was
explanation: According to Acts 28:8, Publius' father lay sick with fever and dysentery; Paul visited him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
proTip: Note the specific ailments healed during Paul's shipwreck stopover in Malta (fever and dysentery).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Mission to the Gentiles / Conclusion of Acts
question: Your blood is upon your heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles." The above statement was made by
explanation: According to Acts 18:6 (and echoed in similar contexts in Acts 13:46 and 28:28), when the Jews in Corinth opposed and reviled him, Paul shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be upon your heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.'
proTip: Track Paul's recurring strategic shift from local Jewish synagogues to the Gentiles when facing intense rejection.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: What was upon the face of the deep on the first day of creation?
explanation: According to the creation narrative in Genesis 1:2, the earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep while the Spirit of God moved over the waters.
proTip: Always distinguish between the initial state of chaos/darkness and the subsequent introduction of light on the first day.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Let there be lights in the firmament of the heavens to separate the day from the night..." This statement was made by God on the
explanation: God created the sun, moon, and stars (the lights in the firmament of heaven) on the fourth day of creation to rule over the day and night and to separate light from darkness (Genesis 1:14-19).
proTip: Memorize the sequence of creation days: days 1-3 form the environment (light, firmament, land/plants), while days 4-6 populate them (luminaries, sea/air creatures, land animals/man).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The story of the Fall teaches that
options: man was made in the image of God
it is a sin to disobey God
Adam was less guilty than Eve
explanation: The narrative of the Fall in Genesis 3 illustrates the core theological truth that rebelling against God's explicit commands brings moral corruption, separation from God, and judgment, emphasizing that disobedience to God is sin.
proTip: Focus on the moral and theological consequence of disobedience rather than circumstantial details when analyzing the Fall.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: 'On that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth and the windows of the heavens were opened.' The result of this was a
explanation: Genesis 7:11-12 describes the cataclysmic flood caused by the breaking up of the fountains of the great deep and the opening of the windows of heaven, resulting in torrential and prolonged rainfall.
proTip: Relate physical descriptions in biblical narratives directly to their climatic or historical outcomes.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would suckle children?..."
explanation: Upon the birth of Isaac, Sarah expressed her joyful astonishment in Genesis 21:7, remarking that no one could have told Abraham that she would nurse children in her old age.
proTip: Pay attention to direct quotes and the specific speakers/context in patriarchal narratives.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The quotation, "Let me not look upon the death of the child" comes from the story about
options: the expulsion of Hagar and Ishmael
Moses when he was placed on the bank of the Nile
explanation: This sentiment reflects the emotional context of King David's grief over the illness and impending death of the child born to him by Bathsheba, which God struck as a judgment for David's sin (2 Samuel 12:15-18).
proTip: Connect character grief and specific tragic phrases to the correct historical narratives in the books of Samuel and Kings.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Joseph's dream about his future leadership of his brothers was fulfilled when he became
options: the second in command of Pharaoh
explanation: Joseph's youthful dreams of his family bowing down to him were ultimately fulfilled when Pharaoh elevated him to become Vizier, or second-in-command over all Egypt, where his brothers bowed before him during the famine.
proTip: Trace prophetic trajectories in Joseph's life from early dreams to their administrative fulfillment.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The children of Israel cried out to God for help in Egypt because
options: Moses failed to look after them
explanation: Exodus 2:23-25 records that the people of Israel groaned because of their servitude and bondage, and their cry for help came up to God, prompting Him to remember His covenant.
proTip: Identify the primary systemic cause of the Israelites' cries in Egypt as intense slave labor and bondage.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?" The above statement was made by
explanation: According to Exodus 14:5, when Pharaoh and his servants realized that the people had fled after being let go, their minds were changed and they regretted releasing their free labor force, leading to their pursuit.
proTip: Carefully track shifts in Pharaoh's attitude and actions recorded during the dramatic crossing of the Red Sea.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The manna which the Israelites left till the morning in disobedience to God
explanation: In Exodus 16:20, Moses commanded the people not to leave any of the manna until morning. Those who disobeyed found that it bred worms and became foul.
proTip: Remember specific textual consequences of disobedience regarding wilderness provisions like manna.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: God gave the ten commandments to the people of Israel because He
options: wanted their days to be long
redeemed them from slavery in Egypt
frowned at those who took His Name in vain
explanation: The prologue to the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2) establishes that God delivered the law because He is the Lord their God who brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
proTip: Always link the giving of the Mosaic covenant and laws to prior divine redemption and grace.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: ..Choose this day whom you will serve... as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." The Israelites' response to the above statement is
options: ..we also will serve the LORD, for He is our God
..cannot serve the LORD, for He is a holy God
..will serve the LORD though He is a jealous God
..cannot put away the foreign gods among us because our fathers served them
explanation: At the covenant renewal at Shechem (Joshua 24:16-18), when Joshua challenged the people to choose their allegiance, the people responded affirmatively that they too would serve the Lord because He brought them out of Egypt.
proTip: Know the historical declarations of commitment made at major covenant renewals led by figures like Joshua.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: God's anger was kindled against Eli and his children because Eli did not
options: train his children in the way of the LORD
apply appropriate sanctions on his children when due
know the gravity of their actions
explanation: 1 Samuel 3:13 highlights that God judged Eli's house because Eli knew about his sons' blasphemous behaviors and corruption yet failed to restrain or properly discipline/punish them.
proTip: Distinguish between mere verbal awareness and active parental discipline in the downfall of Eli.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The prophets whom Saul met at Gibeah-elohim as confirmation that the LORD had anointed him to rule over God's people, were
explanation: When Saul was anointed by Samuel, he met a band of prophets coming down from the high place playing instruments and prophesying in an ecstatic, inspired state, which transformed Saul as the Spirit rushed upon him (1 Samuel 10:5-10).
proTip: Recognize the distinct forms of prophecy in early Israel, characterized by musical bands and ecstatic states during Saul's rise.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: While David was being anointed king, he received
explanation: According to 1 Samuel 16:13, the moment Samuel anointed David in the midst of his brothers, the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon David from that day forward.
proTip: Connect the anointing of leaders in the Old Testament directly with the empowering coming of the Spirit.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Against whom were the Israelites fighting when King David committed adultery with Uriah's wife?
explanation: 2 Samuel 11:1 notes that the incident occurred in the spring of the year when kings go out to battle, specifically when David sent Joab and his servants with all Israel to lay siege against the Ammonites (while Uriah was fighting at Rabbah).
proTip: Always note the military campaign context surrounding David's grave moral failure with Bathsheba.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: According to Psalm 51, the sacrifice acceptable to God is
explanation: Psalm 51:17 declares that the sacrifices acceptable to God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, Thou will not despise.
proTip: Distinguish between ritual sacrifices under the law and the internal spiritual posture emphasized in penitential psalms.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Solomon could devote his attention to the building of the house of the LORD because
options: of the supplies from the Queen of Sheba
there was neither adversary nor misfortune
of David's purchase of the site for the building
explanation: 1 Kings 5:4 records that Solomon stated he was able to build the temple because the Lord his God had given him rest on every side, with neither adversary nor misfortune.
proTip: Recognize the geopolitical stability and peace during early Solomon's reign as a prerequisite for constructing the temple.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The immediate cause of the division of the kingdom was
explanation: While Solomon's idolatry was the underlying cause, the immediate catalyst and trigger for the splitting of the kingdom was Rehoboam's foolish rejection of the elders' advice in favor of harsh taxation and labor burdens (1 Kings 12).
proTip: Differentiate between long-term prophetic causes (Solomon's sin) and the immediate political trigger (Rehoboam's harsh response).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
question: Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and dwell there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to feed you." What exactly necessitated this event?
options: The drought caused by Elijah's curse
Ahab's evil in the sight of the LORD
The ravens ceased to feed Elijah
explanation: Elijah was sent to Zarephath because the brook Cherith dried up as a direct result of the severe nationwide drought that Elijah had declared upon Israel due to Ahab's wickedness (1 Kings 17:1-9).
proTip: Connect prophetic declarations of drought and the drying of natural water sources to God's relocation of His servants.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Birth and Early Life of Jesus (Luke 1-2)
question: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel,..." is a hymn of praise by
options: the Virgin Mary at the Annunciation
Zechariah at the birth of John the Baptist
Simeon at the presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Elizabeth at the visit of Mary
explanation: Known as the Benedictus (Luke 1:68-79), this hymn of praise was uttered by Zechariah (John the Baptist's father) immediately after his speech was restored upon naming his newborn son.
proTip: Associate the Magnificat with Mary, the Benedictus with Zechariah, and the Nunc Dimittis with Simeon.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Birth and Early Life of Jesus (Matthew 2)
question: According to the birth and infancy narratives in St. Matthew, the angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream three times. In the second appearance, he instructed Joseph to
options: accept that Mary was a virgin
explanation: Matthew's gospel records three nocturnal angelic dreams for Joseph: first, to take Mary as wife; second, to flee to Egypt with the child to escape Herod; and third, to return to Israel after Herod's death (Matthew 2:13).
proTip: Track the sequence of Joseph's dreams in Matthew: 1) accept Mary, 2) flee to Egypt, 3) return to Israel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Birth and Early Life of Jesus (Luke 2)
question: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word; for mine eyes have seen thy salvation." This was said at the dedication of Jesus by
explanation: This prayer (the Nunc Dimittis), found in Luke 2:29-32, was spoken by the righteous and devout man Simeon when he took the infant Jesus into his arms at the Temple in Jerusalem.
proTip: Recognize Simeon's prophetic declaration of Jesus as a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory to Israel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?"
explanation: John the Baptist addressed this harsh rebuke to the crowds coming to his baptism, specifically calling out the Pharisees and Sadducees who came to the Jordan without showing genuine fruits of repentance (Matthew 3:7).
proTip: Identify John the Baptist's preaching style, characterized by stern calls for repentance and unsparing rebukes of religious elites.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The second temptation of Jesus according to Luke's account of the gospel was
options: giving the kingdoms of the world to Jesus if he would worship the devil
a command for a stone to become bread
jumping down from the pinnacle of the temple
denying the name of God, the Father
explanation: While Matthew's and Luke's order of the second and third temptations differ slightly, Luke's specific narrative sequence places the devil showing Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and offering them for worship as the second temptation (Luke 4:5-7).
proTip: Note that Luke arranges the temptations climactically with the temple test last, whereas Matthew places the high mountain test last.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: What did Christ say should be the qualification of whoever was to be first or great among the apostles?
options: Giving one's life as a ransom
Drinking from the same cup as Jesus
explanation: In response to the ambition of the sons of Zebedee, Jesus taught that whoever wishes to be great among His followers must be their servant, and whoever wishes to be first among them must be a slave of all (Mark 10:43-44).
proTip: Contradicting worldly structures, Christian leadership in the Gospels is strictly defined through servant-hood.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: A would-be disciple, who puts his hand to the plough and looks back, lacks
explanation: Jesus stated in Luke 9:62 that anyone who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of God, emphasizing the absolute, undivided commitment required for following Him.
proTip: Associate agricultural metaphors used by Jesus in discipleship teachings with the demand for single-minded dedication.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: In which miracle story was Jesus mistaken for a ghost by his disciples?
options: The feeding of the five thousand
Calming of the storm and sea
explanation: When Jesus walked across the stormy sea toward the boat during the night, the disciples were terrified and cried out in fear, supposing that they were seeing a ghost (Mark 6:49).
proTip: Remember that Jesus walking on water prompted both fear of a phantom and Peter's short-lived faith walk.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Luke, the healing of the paralytic was intended to show that
options: Jesus has authority to forgive sins
the Holy Spirit makes intercession for sinners
explanation: Jesus explicitly stated during the healing of the paralytic lowered through the roof that He performed the physical miracle so that the crowd would know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (Luke 5:24).
proTip: Connect Jesus' healing miracles in the Synoptics to His overarching divine authority to forgive spiritual transgressions.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: ..I adjure you by God, do not torment me..." What is the significance of this statement?
options: The demons wanted to reach an agreement with Jesus.
The demons wanted to bargain for their final destination.
It is a recognition of the fact that demons are subject to Jesus.
It shows that demons hate Jesus.
explanation: This plea by the demon-possessed man of Gerasene before Jesus demonstrates that unclean spirits recognize the supreme holiness and divine authority of Christ, knowing they are entirely subject to His command (Mark 5:7).
proTip: Recognize that spiritual forces in the Gospels instantly acknowledge Jesus' divine lordship long before human recognition.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The story of the healing of blind Bartimaeus teaches that
options: prayer is very basic to healing
there is need to persistently shout for attention
Jesus is the Son of David
faith is a pre-requisite to healing
explanation: Upon healing Bartimaeus, Jesus explicitly told him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well," underscoring that active personal faith is the vital conduit for receiving divine healing (Mark 10:52).
proTip: Always link healing outcomes in Jesus' ministry directly to the recipient's personal expression of faith.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The parable of the prodigal son emphasizes that
options: it is not good for the son and the father to quarrel
the father loves the second son more than the first
explanation: The core theological emphasis of the Prodigal Son parable is God's profound readiness to forgive, embrace, and celebrate sinners who experience a genuine heart repentance and return to Him (Luke 15:20-24).
proTip: Focus on divine mercy, repentance, and restoration as the central themes of Luke 15 parables.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Matthew's account of the gospel, the most important divine requirement for entering the kingdom of heaven is
explanation: In Matthew 7:21, Jesus states unequivocally that not everyone who calls Him Lord will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of His Father in heaven.
proTip: Distinguish between outward religious profession and active obedience to God's will as emphasized in the Sermon on the Mount.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: After their mission, the seventy disciplines reported to Jesus that
options: they enjoyed the hospitality of people
demons were subject to them in His name
explanation: Luke 10:17 records that the seventy returned with joy, exclaiming, "Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!"
proTip: Note the specific success metric reported by the seventy missionaries regarding spiritual authority over demonic forces.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The appearance of Moses and Elijah at the transfiguration underscores the importance in the ministry of Jesus of
explanation: Moses represented the Law and Elijah represented the Prophets; their appearance with Jesus on the mount signifies that Jesus fulfills the entire Old Testament revelation contained in the Law and the Prophets.
proTip: Always associate Moses with the Law and Elijah with the Prophets when analyzing their appearance at the Transfiguration.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: This is my beloved Son; listen to him." This was said on the occasion of Jesus'
explanation: A bright cloud overshadowed the disciples during the Transfiguration, and a voice from the cloud spoke these exact words, commanding obedience to Jesus (Matthew 17:5, Mark 9:7, Luke 9:35).
proTip: Note that while a similar heavenly voice spoke at Jesus' baptism, the specific command "listen to Him" was given during the Transfiguration.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing (Mark 11 / Luke 19)
question: My house shall be a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers." Just before making this statement, the speaker
options: drove out those who sold in the temple
explanation: In cleansing the temple during His triumphal week, Jesus physically overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling pigeons, driving out those who commercialized the sacred space before rebuking them with this scripture (Mark 11:15-17).
proTip: Connect Jesus' righteous indignation in the temple courts directly with His cleansing action against commercial exploitation.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Trials and Death of Jesus (Matthew 26 / Mark 14)
question: Which of the following questions did the high priest ask Jesus during His trial?
options: Are you the Christ, the son of the Blessed?
Are you the King of the Jews?
Are you the Son of David?
explanation: During His religious trial before the Sanhedrin, the high priest directly asked Jesus, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" to which Jesus gave His affirmative confession (Mark 14:61).
proTip: Distinguish between the religious trial question asked by the High Priest (Son of the Blessed) and the political trial question asked by Pilate (King of the Jews).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children..." These words were addressed by Jesus to the
explanation: As Jesus was led away to be crucified, He turned to the lamenting women following Him along the path to Calvary and addressed them as the "daughters of Jerusalem," warning them of future judgment (Luke 23:28).
proTip: Pay attention to specific demographic groups addressed by Jesus during His journey to the cross in Luke's Gospel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: What was the first statement of Jesus on the cross according to Luke's account of the gospel?
options: Today you shall be with me in paradise.
Father forgive them for they do not know what they do.
explanation: Luke's unique recording of Jesus' sayings on the cross opens with His intercessory prayer for His executioners: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34).
proTip: Memorize the unique 'seven last words' attributed to Jesus across the different Gospels, noting Luke's inclusion of the prayer for forgiveness.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Very early in the morning, on the first day of the week, three women went to the tomb of Jesus to
options: see whether the soldiers had carried the body away
explanation: According to the Gospel accounts (such as Mark 16:1-2 and Luke 24:1), the women went to the tomb early on the first day of the week bearing spices they had prepared in order to anoint Jesus' dead body.
proTip: Distinguish between the women's initial intention (burial anointing) and their subsequent discovery of the empty tomb.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: ..Let all the house of Israel therefore know assuredly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified..." As a reaction to this declaration, the Jews
options: decided to kill Peter and the apostles
went back to their houses in anger
were deeply troubled and asked what they should do
explanation: Acts 2:37 records that upon hearing Peter's powerful Pentecost sermon convicting them of crucifying Jesus, the listeners were cut to the heart and asked Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brethren, what shall we do?"
proTip: Connect conviction under the preaching of the Word in Acts 2 directly with repentance and the inquiry about salvation.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: You have not lied to men but to God." The immediate effect of this statement of Peter on the liar was that he
explanation: When Peter confronted Ananias regarding his deceit over the proceeds of property sold in Acts 5:3-5, Ananias immediately fell down dead upon hearing these words, striking great fear into all who heard it.
proTip: Remember the divine judgment on hypocrisy and dishonesty within the primitive Christian community in Acts.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Fellowship in the Early Church / Deacons (Acts 6)
question: The apostles created a new office in the ministry besides prayer and preaching, in order to address the problems of
explanation: The appointment of the seven deacons in Acts 6 was necessitated by administrative inequality and discrimination (injustice) in the daily distribution of food to the Hellenistic widows compared to the Hebrew widows.
proTip: Associate the appointment of the seven deacons with resolving social inequity and administrative neglect in the early church.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Opposition to the Gospel / Conversion of Paul (Acts 9)
question: Saul's encounter with the Risen Christ on the road to Damascus convinced him that
options: Jesus is the Son of God
the faith of his father was right
he should have gone to Damascus with more armed escort
explanation: The dramatic heavenly vision and voice of Jesus on the Damascus road fundamentally transformed Saul, proving to him irrefutably that Jesus of Nazareth is indeed the living Son of God (Acts 9:5-20).
proTip: Understand Paul's conversion as the pivot from persecuting the church to proclaiming Jesus as the Son of God.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: When Saul escaped from Damascus to Jerusalem after his conversion, the disciples in Jerusalem
options: were full of sympathy for him
explanation: Acts 9:26 states that when Saul arrived in Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was actually a genuine disciple until Barnabas vouched for him.
proTip: Note the initial skepticism and fear displayed by the Jerusalem believers toward newly converted Saul.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Paul and Barnabas were referred to as 'gods' in Lystra because they
options: were agents of the unknown God
explanation: After Paul miraculously healed a man who had been crippled from birth in Lystra, the pagan crowd became ecstatic and shouted in Lycaonian that the gods had come down to them, calling Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes (Acts 14:8-12).
proTip: Connect miraculous physical healing events in Acts to immediate cultural or pagan misinterpretations by crowds.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Mission to the Gentiles / Jerusalem Council (Acts 15)
question: ..Abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols and from blood and from what is strangled and from unchastity.." To which issue was the above a response?
explanation: These four practical guidelines were the formal resolution issued by the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:20-29) to resolve the intense circumcision controversy and fellowship friction between Jewish and Gentile believers.
proTip: Associate the Jerusalem Council decrees directly with settling the terms of Gentile inclusion without requiring circumcision.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Opposition to the Gospel / Trials of Paul (Acts 23)
question: ..I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; with respect to the hope and resurrection of the dead I am on trial." This was part of the address of Paul to
explanation: Paul delivered this strategic defense before the divided council of the Sanhedrin in Acts 23:6, pitting the Pharisees against the Sadducees over the doctrine of the resurrection.
proTip: Recognize Paul's tactical use of theological division (resurrection belief) when standing trial before the Sanhedrin.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to Paul, which of the following is the greatest?
explanation: In his renowned discourse on spiritual gifts and Christian virtues in 1 Corinthians 13:13, Paul concludes that faith, hope, and love abide, these three, but the greatest of these is love.
proTip: Memorize 1 Corinthians 13:13 as the definitive scriptural hierarchy of Christian theological virtues.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: According to the creation account of Genesis 1, God charged man to
options: have dominion over all the earth
explanation: In Genesis 1:28, after creating mankind in His image, God blessed them and charged them to be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and have dominion over every living thing.
proTip: Remember that the Genesis 1 creation mandate emphasizes stewardship, fruitfulness, and dominion over creation.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Flood and Judgment / Sanctity of Life (Genesis 9)
question: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for God made man in his own image." This statement explains the
explanation: This post-flood ordinance given to Noah (Genesis 9:6) underscores the supreme sanctity and high value of human life because human beings are created in the image of God.
proTip: Always link capital accountability for murder directly back to the theological doctrine of the imago Dei (image of God).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: When God told Abraham that Sarah would have a child, Abraham laughed because
options: they were too old to have a child
he already had a child called Ishmael.
explanation: According to Genesis 17:17, when God promised that Sarah would bear a son, Abraham fell on his face and laughed, thinking to himself whether a child could be born to a man a hundred years old and whether Sarah, who was ninety, could bear a child.
proTip: Distinguish between Abraham's internal reaction of incredulity due to advanced age and Sarah's subsequent laughter behind the tent door.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: After Jacob's dream at Bethel, he promised that he would
options: give a tenth of all he would have to God
return immediately and settle there with his family
go to his father's house in peace.
explanation: In Genesis 28:20-22, following his vision of the ladder at Bethel, Jacob made a vow that if God would watch over him and bring him back safely, he would make the Lord his God and give a tenth of all God gave him.
proTip: Associate Jacob's vow at Bethel with the biblical precedent for tithing and acknowledgment of God's provision.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Why did Judah advise his brother against shedding the blood of Joseph?
options: He wanted to raise some money by selling Joseph.
explanation: When the brothers plotted to kill Joseph, Judah intervened in Genesis 37:26-27 by persuading them to sell him to the Ishmaelites instead, emphasizing, 'He is our brother, our own flesh.'
proTip: Recognize Judah's pragmatic yet family-conscious intervention that spared Joseph's life.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Why did God redeem the Israelites from the hands of Pharaoh?
options: God remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
They yoke of the Israelites was heavy
God wanted to show His power to Pharaoh
He wanted to show that Moses was powerful
explanation: Exodus 2:24 and Exodus 6:5 explicitly state that God heard the groaning of the Israelites and remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which served as the foundational basis for their redemption.
proTip: Always link God's acts of deliverance in the Pentateuch back to His foundational covenant promises to the patriarchs.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: When the people of Israel saw the great work of the LORD in drowning the Egyptians, they
options: built an altar to the LORD
explanation: Following the miraculous crossing of the Red Sea and the destruction of the Egyptian pursuers, Exodus 14:31 records that Israel saw the great power of the Lord, and they feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in His servant Moses.
proTip: Connect major miraculous deliverances in the wilderness narrative with temporary spikes in public faith and reverence for God's appointed leaders.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The golden calf which Aaron made for the people of Israel signified
options: a return to the gods of Egypt.
the final break with the god that brought them out of Egypt.
the beginning of idolatry in Israel
the end of Moses' leadership of the people of Israel.
explanation: The creation of the golden calf represented a dangerous syncretistic relapse into the idolatrous practices and animal worship (such as Apis or Mnevis bulls) common in Egypt, breaking the newly established covenant command.
proTip: Recognize the golden calf incident as a prime biblical example of syncretism and rebellion shortly after covenant establishment.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: During the giving of the law at Mount Sinai, the Israelites wanted Moses to speak to them instead of God because
options: the people were afraid and trembled
explanation: According to Exodus 20:18-19 and Deuteronomy 5:25-26, when the people witnessed the thunder, lightning, trumpet blast, and smoking mountain, they were terrified and begged Moses to speak to them instead of God, fearing that otherwise they would die.
proTip: Note the overwhelming terror and holiness experienced by the Israelites at Sinai, establishing the need for a mediator.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Where did Joshua gather all the tribes of Israel for presentation before God?
explanation: Joshua 24:1 states that Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem, summoning their elders, heads, judges, and officers to present themselves before God for the great covenant renewal ceremony.
proTip: Always associate Joshua's final farewell address and covenant renewal ceremony with the historical site of Shechem.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The valley of Eshcol is symbolic to Israel because it was the place where
options: Moses and his people had a resounding victory over the Amalekites
the men of Israel cut down the cluster of grapes
the spies set out to survey Canaan
the Israelites challenged the leadership of Moses and Aaron.
explanation: Numbers 13:23-24 records that when the spies explored the land, they came to the Valley of Eshcol and cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes so heavy it had to be carried on a pole by two men.
proTip: Associate Eshcol with the physical evidence of the land's abundance brought back by the spies.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The report brought by the men who followed Caleb to spy the land of Canaan showed that the land
explanation: While the majority report focused on fortified cities and giants, the faithful spies demonstrated the tangible proof that the land indeed flowed with milk and honey by displaying its rich fruits (Numbers 13:27).
proTip: Distinguish between the pessimistic fear-based report of the ten spies and the faith-filled report emphasizing the land's richness.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The Shema emphasizes the
options: importance of Israel to the world,
explanation: The Shema ("Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one" - Deuteronomy 6:4) is the foundational confession of monotheism in Judaism, emphasizing the absolute unity and uniqueness of Yahweh.
proTip: Memorize Deuteronomy 6:4 as the core scriptural pillar establishing monotheism and the unity of God.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Parental Responsibility / Hannah and Samuel (1 Samuel 1)
question: The LORD give you children by this woman for the loan which she lent to the LORD;..."
explanation: This blessing was pronounced by Eli the priest upon Elkanah after Hannah dedicated her promised son Samuel to the service of the Lord at Shiloh, resulting in God blessing Hannah with more children (1 Samuel 2:20).
proTip: Link this blessing directly to the dedication of Samuel at the sanctuary in Shiloh.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Parental Responsibility / Eli vs Samuel (1 Samuel 2-3)
question: A good example of parental upbringing is manifested in the son of
explanation: While Eli failed to discipline his wicked sons Hophni and Phinehas, and David struggled with family governance, Samuel's early dedication and righteous upbringing stand in stark contrast—though his own sons later stumbled, Samuel's personal integrity and upbringing in the house of the Lord represent the intended ideal in this comparative context.
proTip: Contrast Eli's disastrous failure in parental discipline with faithful figures in early Israelite narratives.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The leadership potential of David was demonstrated publicly for the first time when he
options: spared King Saul's life into he cave
explanation: Although anointed privately by Samuel earlier, David's public emergence as a national champion and leader before all Israel occurred when he defeated the Philistine giant Goliath in single combat (1 Samuel 17).
proTip: Distinguish between private prophetic anointing and the public milestone of defeating Goliath that launched David into national prominence.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Although David refused to kill Saul because he was the LORD'S anointed, he still believed that
options: Saul would be killed by the Philistines
the LORD would eventually smite Saul
Saul's soldiers would cause him to die in battle.,
explanation: In 1 Samuel 26:10, when sparing Saul a second time in the wilderness of Ziph, David declared, 'As the Lord lives, the Lord will strike him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall go down into battle and perish.'
proTip: Note David's profound respect for divine timing regarding God's anointed, leaving vengeance entirely in God's hands.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Blessed be you, my son David! You will do many things and will succeed in them", the above statement was made when David
explanation: This exclamation was uttered by King Saul in 1 Samuel 24:19 after David spared his life in the cave at Engedi and demonstrated his loyalty by refusing to harm the Lord's anointed.
proTip: Connect Saul's temporary remorse and blessings bestowed upon David directly to instances where David spared his life.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Solomon asked God for wisdom to enable him
explanation: When God offered Solomon whatever he desired at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:9), Solomon asked for an understanding mind (wisdom) to govern God's people and to discern between good and evil.
proTip: Remember that Solomon's request for judicial discernment and wisdom pleased God because he did not ask for long life, wealth, or the death of enemies.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The consequence of Rehoboam's unwise decision at the time the Israelites came to him at Shechem eventually resulted in
explanation: Rehoboam's harsh rejection of the people's plea for lighter labor at Shechem immediately triggered the tribal rebellion led by Jeroboam, permanently splitting the united monarchy into the northern kingdom of Israel and southern kingdom of Judah (1 Kings 12:16-20).
proTip: Trace the political fracture of Israel directly back to Rehoboam's rejection of wise elders' counsel in favor of oppression.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile
question: The new covenant which God was to make with the house of Israel was that it would be
options: for the tribe of Judah alone
explanation: Jeremiah 31:33 prophesied that under the New Covenant, God would put His law within His people and write it upon their hearts, rather than merely on external tablets of stone.
proTip: Contrast the external Mosaic covenant on stone tablets with the internal heart transformation promised in Jeremiah's New Covenant.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Luke, John the Baptist instructed the multitudes that came to be baptized to
options: give thanks for being Abraham's children.
explanation: Luke 3:8 records John telling the crowds coming for baptism, 'Bear fruits that befit repentance,' explaining that physical lineage from Abraham was insufficient without practical ethical transformation.
proTip: Associate John the Baptist's ethical demands with practical social acts of charity and justice reflecting true repentance.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Birth and Early Life of Jesus (Matthew 2)
question: Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him bring me word...." The intention of the speaker in this context was to
options: pay homage to the Lord Jesus
kill all the children in the area
explanation: King Herod instructed the wise men with this deceitful request in Matthew 2:8, intending to locate the infant Jesus so he could eliminate Him as a perceived rival to his throne.
proTip: Recognize the deceptive political motives behind Herod's inquiry regarding the birthplace of the Messiah.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus was tempted in the wilderness in order to
options: proved that He was the Son of God
prepare Him for His earthly ministry
explanation: The temptation of Jesus immediately following His baptism served as the crucial spiritual crucible and preparation that equipped Him to inaugurate and successfully execute His public ministry in total obedience to God.
proTip: View the wilderness temptation as the qualification and spiritual testing ground for Jesus' public messianic mission.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: One important fact about Mary brought out in Jesus miracle of changing water to wine was that she
options: must intercede for a miracle to occur
was a sister of the bridegroom
had a deep insight of her son and His ability.
explanation: During the wedding at Cana (John 2:3-5), Mary's immediate appeal to Jesus when the wine ran out and her instruction to the servants ('Do whatever he tells you') demonstrated her profound maternal insight into His divine capabilities.
proTip: Note Mary's implicit trust in Jesus' supernatural power during the crisis at the Cana wedding.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The raising of Lazarus illustrates that Jesus
options: was a good friend of Lazarus
explanation: The climactic miracle of raising Lazarus from the dead four days after burial serves in John's Gospel as the living proof of Jesus' declaration 'I am the resurrection and the life,' demonstrating His absolute divine power over death.
proTip: Connect the Lazarus miracle directly to Jesus' theological claim as the author of eternal life and resurrection.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, ..." The continuation of this message by the centurion indicated that
options: he had faith in the power of Jesus' word
as a Gentile, he did not like the Jews
as an army officer, he wanted to avoid contact with Jesus.
explanation: The Roman centurion's famous statement (Luke 7:6-8) expressed his profound understanding of spiritual authority, believing that Jesus did not need to be physically present but could heal his servant merely by speaking a word from a distance.
proTip: Recognize the centurion's extraordinary faith in the autonomous power of Jesus' spoken word, which amazed Jesus Himself.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The epileptic boy could not be healed by the disciples because
options: they had not ye received power
their prayers were not intensive enough
they had to wait for Jesus
explanation: When the disciples asked why they failed to cast out the demonic spirit causing epilepsy, Jesus rebuked their lack of faith and explained in Mark 9:29 that this kind can come out only by prayer (and fasting).
proTip: Link discipleship failures in exorcism and healing directly to lapses in spiritual discipline, reliance, and faith.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The poor in spirit are promised
explanation: In Luke's version of the Beatitudes (Luke 6:20), Jesus declares, 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God' (corresponding to 'poor in spirit' in Matthew 5:3).
proTip: Memorize the specific beatitude pairings and their corresponding kingdom promises across Matthew and Luke.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Those that are hated and reviled shall
options: have a great reward in heaven
explanation: Luke 6:22-23 encourages disciples who are hated, excluded, reviled, and defamed for the Son of Man's sake to rejoice and leap for joy, because behold, their reward is great in heaven.
proTip: Connect perseverance under persecution with heavenly rewards in the Beatitudes.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus' objective for sending out the twelve was
options: for them to teach the Gentiles about the God of the Jews
to train the disciples in His ministry
to demonstrate that He was about to be crucified
to divert the attention of Herod from Himself.
explanation: Sending out the disciples on mission tours served as practical, hands-on training where they participated directly in preaching, healing, and casting out demons under Jesus' authority, preparing them for post-ascension leadership.
proTip: View the missionary journeys of the disciples as practical field training in kingdom ministry.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Who appeared and talked with Jesus during the transfiguration?
explanation: All three synoptic gospels record that during the Transfiguration, Moses (representing the Law) and Elijah (representing the Prophets) appeared in glory and conversed with Jesus regarding His impending departure (Luke 9:30-31).
proTip: Always pair Moses and Elijah together as the Old Testament representatives at the Transfiguration.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Great us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory..." Why was this request by the sons of Zebedee not granted?
options: They were not qualified for the privilege
The other disciplines disagreed with them
They were unable to drink the cup
It was not the duty of Jesus to grant their request.
explanation: In Mark 10:40, Jesus rebuffed James and John's ambitious request by stating that granting seats of honor at His right and left is not His to give, but is for those for whom it has been prepared by His Father.
proTip: Note that divine authority over heavenly rewards rests ultimately with God the Father.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing (Mark 11 / Luke 19)
question: Where did Jesus lodge after he cleansed the temple?
explanation: Mark 11:11 records that after entering Jerusalem, looking around at everything, and cleansing the temple, Jesus went out to Bethany with the twelve because it was late.
proTip: Associate Bethany as the resting place and lodging village for Jesus during the intense days of Passion week.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Trials and Death of Jesus (Luke 23 / John 18)
question: At the trials of Jesus, Pilate was perplexed because
options: the Jews had no genuine case against Him
Jesus gave no answer to the charges
the Jews asked for the release of Barabbas, a notorious criminal
he knew that Jesus had performed many miracles among the Jews.,
explanation: During His trial before Pilate and Herod, Jesus' majestic silence and refusal to answer multiple accusations in self-defense astonished and perplexed the Roman governors (Matthew 27:14, Mark 15:5).
proTip: Recognize Jesus' deliberate silence under interrogation as the fulfillment of Isaiah's suffering servant prophecy.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Why did the accusers of Jesus stay behind while He was led to the Praetorium?
options: It was forbidden to follow the accused
They did not want to be defiled.
explanation: According to John 18:28, the Jewish leaders did not enter Pilate's headquarters (Praetorium) so that they would not be ceremonially defiled, but could still eat the Passover.
proTip: Notice the bitter irony of religious leaders meticulously guarding ritual purity laws while plotting judicial murder.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Trials and Death of Jesus (Luke 23 / Mark 15)
question: Who was forced to carry the cross behind Jesus?
explanation: As Jesus was led out to be crucified, the Roman soldiers seized Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26, Mark 15:21).
proTip: Remember that Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry the cross beam when Jesus grew physically exhausted.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise".
explanation: Jesus spoke this comforting promise from the cross to the repentant criminal crucified beside Him who rebuked the mocking robber and asked Jesus to remember Him when He came into His kingdom (Luke 23:43).
proTip: Associate this famous dying promise exclusively with the repentant thief on the cross.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Luke, the people who first got to Jesus' tomb were
options: Mary the mother of Jesus, Peter and John
Mary Magdalene and the other women
explanation: Luke 24:1, 10 records that the women who came from Galilee (including Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James) were the first to arrive at the tomb early on the first day of the week with the spices they had prepared.
proTip: Note that across the Gospels, women disciples were consistently the earliest witnesses to the empty tomb.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus Christ, the Good Shepherd was loved by the Father because He
options: understood the needs of the sheep
laid down His life for the sheep.
explanation: In John 10:17, Jesus explicitly states, 'For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again,' highlighting sacrificial atonement as the supreme expression of His pastoral obedience.
proTip: Connect the Father's love for the Good Shepherd directly to His voluntary sacrifice of laying down His life.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: But you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth. This statement commissions the apostles to
options: establish the church in Jewish cities
carry the gospel to all continents
preach to the Gentiles in and outside Palestine
explanation: Acts 1:8 outlines the strategic geographical roadmap for Christian expansion, moving from Jerusalem outward through Judea, Samaria, and ultimately to the remotest parts of the earth (global mission).
proTip: Use Acts 1:8 as the foundational thematic blueprint for the entire book of Acts and global Christian missions.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life: he who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and whoever lives and believes in me shall never die... On what occasion was this statement made?
options: On the day of Jesus resurrection
When Jesus demonstrated the fact of His resurrection to Thomas
On the day Jesus restored Lazarus back to life
When Jairus daughter was raised from the dead.
explanation: Jesus made this profound declaration to Martha outside Bethany just before performing the miracle of raising her brother Lazarus from the dead (John 11:25).
proTip: Associate the 'I am the resurrection and the life' pronouncement directly with the narrative of raising Lazarus.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to Paul, if we give away all that we and we deliver our bodies to be burnt, but have not love we
explanation: 1 Corinthians 13:3 emphasizes that even extreme acts of charity (giving away all possessions) or supreme martyrdom (surrendering one's body to be burned) profit nothing if motivated by anything other than genuine agape love.
proTip: Remember that love is portrayed in 1 Corinthians 13 as the indispensable prerequisite giving value to all spiritual gifts and sacrifices.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Now the company of those who believed were of one hart and soul..." This reveals that the early Christians
options: were always filled with the Holy Spirit.
explanation: Acts 4:32 describes the remarkable unity of the primitive Jerusalem church, noting that no one claimed private ownership of their possessions, but they held everything in common.
proTip: Connect 'one heart and soul' in early church descriptions with radical economic sharing and communal harmony.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Fellowship in the Early Church / Deacons (Acts 6)
question: The suggestion to choose the seven deacons was made by
explanation: Acts 6:2 records that the twelve apostles summoned the body of the disciples together to propose appointing the seven deacons so that the apostles could remain devoted to prayer and ministry of the word.
proTip: Attribute the administrative initiative of appointing the seven deacons to the twelve apostles.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and you're your men shall see visions..." This prophecy was fulfilled
explanation: Peter quoted this exact messianic prophecy of Joel during his landmark sermon on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21) to explain the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and speaking in tongues.
proTip: Always associate Joel's outpouring of the Spirit with the events of Acts 2 at Pentecost.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
subTopic: New Life in Christ / Faith of the Patriarchs (Hebrews 11)
question: Who are the men of old mentioned as examples of faith in the Letter to the Hebrews?
explanation: Hebrews 11 (the great hall of faith) lists numerous Old Testament figures who gained divine approval through faith, explicitly featuring Abel, Abraham, Rahab, Enoch, Noah, and Moses.
proTip: Recognize Hebrews 11 as the definitive biblical roster illustrating justification and endurance by faith.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to James, effective prayer is that which is offered
explanation: James 1:6 and James 5:15 emphasize that approaching God in prayer must be done in steadfast faith without doubting, as the prayer offered in faith will save the sick and accomplish great things.
proTip: Connect answered prayer in James' epistle directly to the prerequisite of unwavering faith.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
subTopic: Christian Living in the Community / Impartiality (1 Peter 2)
question: According to Peter, Christians living among non-Christians should
explanation: 1 Peter 2:12 exhorts believers to maintain excellent conduct among the Gentiles (non-Christians) so that, even though they speak against them as evildoers, they may see their good deeds and glorify God.
proTip: Note Peter's emphasis on exemplary civic and moral conduct as a silent witness to unbelievers.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
subTopic: Civic Responsibility / Obedience to Authority (1 Peter 2 / Romans 13)
question: Peter enjoins Christians to be good citizens by
options: using their freedom to fight for their right
explanation: 1 Peter 2:13-17 commands believers to submit themselves for the Lord's sake to every human institution and governing authority, honoring everyone and respecting civil leadership.
proTip: Associate apostolic epistles with consistent calls for peaceful submission to governing authorities as part of Christian witness.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Elijah at the brook Cherith (1 Kings 17:1-6)
question: When Elijah escaped to the brook Cherith, he was fed by
explanation: After Elijah announced the drought, God told him to hide by the brook Cherith. 1 Kings 17:4-6 says God commanded the ravens to feed him, and they brought him bread and meat morning and evening.
proTip: God can use unlikely means to provide for His servants.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Elijah and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:20-40)
question: The contest on Mount Carmel was to prove that
options: Baal was the god of Israel
God was supreme to other gods
explanation: Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal to a test by fire. When the fire fell on his sacrifice, the people cried, 'The LORD, He is God' (1 Kings 18:39). The contest therefore established the supremacy of the LORD over Baal and all other gods.
proTip: Carmel is the classic text for the Supremacy of God: Baal was silent, the LORD answered.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Naboth did not agree to release his vineyard to Ahab because
options: the amount offered for it was too small
it was his major source of income
it was the inheritance of his fathers
explanation: Naboth replied, 'The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers' (1 Kings 21:3). Under the Law, ancestral land was not to be sold permanently (Leviticus 25:23).
proTip: Remember Naboth's phrase 'inheritance of my fathers' - it explains his refusal, not money or income.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: What did Gehazi, the deceitful servant, receive from Naaman?
options: two talents of silver and two festal garments
two talents of silver and two shekels of gold
two festal garments and two talents of gold
two thousand shekels and two festal garments
explanation: Gehazi ran after Naaman and lied that two young men had come to Elisha, asking for a talent of silver and two festal garments. Naaman gave him two talents of silver in two bags with two festal garments (2 Kings 5:22-23). Gehazi was struck with Naaman's leprosy as punishment.
proTip: Gehazi is the standard example of greed and its effects: silver, garments, then leprosy.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Religious reforms in Judah - King Josiah (2 Kings 22-23)
question: The greatest achievement of King Josiah of Judah was his
options: sweeping reforms of the religious life of his people
training a worthy successor before his death
explanation: After the Book of the Law was found in the Temple, Josiah renewed the covenant, destroyed idols, high places and pagan altars, and restored the Passover (2 Kings 23:1-25). The Temple repair was done, but his reform of worship is his best-known achievement.
proTip: Josiah = discovery of the Book of the Law + covenant renewal + sweeping religious reform.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Jerusalem fell in 586 B.C. to the Babylonian king called
explanation: 2 Kings 25 records that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon besieged and captured Jerusalem, burned the Temple, and carried the people into exile. Asshurbanapal was Assyrian; Psammetichus I was Egyptian.
proTip: Associate 586 B.C. with Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian exile.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: And the king (Artaxerxes) said to me, 'Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing else but sadness of the heart.' Why was the addressee sad?
options: The condition of Jerusalem was deplorable
He was fasting because of Jerusalem
Enemies of Jerusalem were laughing at him
He was in exile in Babylon
explanation: Nehemiah explained that the city where his fathers were buried lay waste and its gates were destroyed by fire (Nehemiah 2:3). His sadness arose from the ruined state of Jerusalem.
proTip: Nehemiah's concern for Judah began with grief over the state of Jerusalem, then led to action.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Although Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were cast into the fiery furnace, King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished to see four men in the furnace. He said the fourth man was like
explanation: Daniel 3:25 (RSV) reads: 'the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.' Nebuchadnezzar saw them unbound and unharmed, and later credited God with sending His angel to deliver them (3:28).
proTip: Match the RSV wording: 'a son of the gods'. The three men show faith, courage and divine protection.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: In the belly of the fish Jonah prayed to God to
explanation: Jonah's prayer from the fish (Jonah 2:1-9) is a cry of distress and thanksgiving, ending 'Deliverance belongs to the LORD' (2:9). He was asking to be rescued from the deep.
