proTip: In Jonah 2 the keyword is deliverance - Jonah is rescued, then recommissioned.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: The sins of Nineveh notwithstanding, God spared the inhabitants because
options: Jonah was reluctant to deliver the message to them
the people responded positively to God's mercy
Nineveh was made up of a large population which did not know its right from its left
Nineveh was a great and prosperous city with one hundred and twenty thousand inhabitants
explanation: When the Ninevites believed God, proclaimed a fast and turned from their evil ways, 'God repented of the evil which he had said he would do to them' (Jonah 3:5-10). God's sparing was in response to their repentance.
proTip: Repentance moves God to mercy; this is the central lesson of Jonah.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Daniel was distinguished above all other satraps and presidents because he
options: had an excellent spirit in him
refused to worship the golden image
explanation: Daniel 6:3 states that Daniel distinguished himself above all other presidents and satraps because an excellent spirit was in him, and the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.
proTip: Quote Daniel 6:3: 'an excellent spirit was in him'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Daniel could not be harmed by the lions because
options: an angel shut the mouths of the lions
a pillar of cloud separated Daniel from the lions
explanation: Daniel told the king, 'My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, and they have not hurt me, because I was found blameless before him' (Daniel 6:22).
proTip: Daniel's protection came from God through His angel, because he was blameless.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Obedience and disobedience - the period of the Judges (Judges 2:11; 3:7)
question: The Israelites did evil in the eyes of the LORD in the days of the Judges by
explanation: Judges 2:11 says Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals; 3:7 repeats that they forgot the LORD and served the Baals and the Asherahs. This apostasy began the repeated cycle of sin, oppression, cry for help and deliverance.
proTip: The cycle in Judges: sin (idolatry), oppression, repentance, deliverance.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice and true religion - Amos 2:6
question: Selling the needy for a pair of shoes in Amos means
options: equating human beings with material things
explanation: In Amos 2:6 the charge is that the righteous are sold for silver and the needy for a pair of shoes. This pictures the powerful exploiting the poor, enslaving them over trivial debts. It is a charge of oppression, a central concern of Amos's message on social justice.
proTip: Amos condemns oppression of the poor by the rich - look for the 'oppression' option.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice and true religion - Amos 2:6-8
question: 'Thus says the LORD: "For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment..."' In the latter part of this prophecy, Amos condemned Israel for
options: not remembering the covenant of brotherhood
rejecting the laws and statutes of the LORD
explanation: After condemning the neighbouring nations, Amos turned to Israel (2:6ff). The charges that follow are social: selling the righteous and needy, trampling the poor, sexual abuse, and holding garments taken in pledge. Rejecting the Law (2:4) was the charge against Judah; the covenant of brotherhood (1:9) was the charge against Tyre.
proTip: Distinguish the nations: Tyre = broken brotherhood covenant; Judah = rejected the Law; Israel = social injustice.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice and true religion - Hosea 6:6
question: From Hosea's teaching, we learn that God
options: will pour His Spirit on all flesh
will create a new heart in His people
prefers knowledge of God to burnt offerings
explanation: Hosea 6:6 reads: 'For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God, rather than burnt offerings.' God wants loyal love and true knowledge of Him over empty ritual. (Note: options C and D were identical in the source scan; D has been reconstructed from the second half of Hosea 6:6.)
proTip: Hosea's core message: covenant love (hesed) over ritual.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Holiness and divine call - Isaiah's teaching
question: The central theme of Isaiah's teachings is that
options: the vilest sinner will not be redeemed
explanation: Isaiah 1:18 says, 'though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.' Isaiah calls for repentance and promises that God can forgive and restore, though not that every sinner is automatically saved.
proTip: Isaiah: sin is serious, but no sinner is beyond God's redemption if he repents.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' Then I said, 'Here am I! Send me.' Why did Isaiah offer himself to be God's messenger?
options: Because the king had died and he needed another job
Having been cleansed of his sins, he saw the need to warn others
Because he had seen the beauty of heaven and wanted to work for God
explanation: In his vision Isaiah confessed his uncleanness, and a seraph touched his lips with a burning coal and declared his guilt taken away (Isaiah 6:5-7). Only after this cleansing did he volunteer (6:8).
proTip: Isaiah's call sequence: vision, confession, cleansing, commission.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Who, according to Ezekiel, did the exiles blame for their plight?
explanation: The exiles quoted a proverb: 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge' (Ezekiel 18:2). Ezekiel taught that each person is responsible for his own sin.
proTip: Ezekiel 18 = individual responsibility, against the idea of inherited guilt.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: God told Jeremiah that He would give Jerusalem into the hands of the Chaldeans because the Israelites
options: did not prepare adequately for war
explanation: Jeremiah 32:29-32 says the city would be given to the Chaldeans because of the evil of Israel and Judah, who 'provoked me to anger' with idolatry, including burning incense to Baal.
proTip: Judgment on Jerusalem came because of the people's persistent sin and idolatry.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: The expression 'dry bones' in Ezekiel refers to
explanation: God explained to Ezekiel, 'these bones are the whole house of Israel' (Ezekiel 37:11). The vision of the bones coming to life promised the restoration of the exiled nation.
proTip: Dry bones = Israel in exile; the vision is a message of hope and national restoration.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to Paul, the law and the prophets bear witness to the
explanation: Romans 3:21 says that the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from law, 'although the law and the prophets bear witness to it.'
proTip: Romans 3:21-22: God's righteousness is received through faith in Jesus Christ.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to Paul in his Letter to the Galatians, one is justified by
explanation: Galatians 2:16: 'a man is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.'
proTip: Paul's formula: justification by faith, not by works of the law.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: The function of the law to believers before the coming of Christ was that of a
explanation: Galatians 3:24 (RSV): 'the law was our custodian until Christ came, that we might be justified by faith.' The law guided and restrained until faith in Christ came.
proTip: RSV uses 'custodian' (Greek paidagogos), a guardian, not a judge.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Justification by grace shows that works are
explanation: Ephesians 2:8-9: 'by grace you have been saved through faith... not because of works, lest any man should boast.' Salvation is a gift, so human works cannot earn it.
proTip: Grace = unearned gift. Good works are the result of salvation, not its cause.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: All Christians who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized
explanation: Romans 6:3: 'all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.' Baptism symbolizes dying to sin and rising to new life.
proTip: Baptism in Romans 6 = union with Christ's death, burial and resurrection.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: In what way did God condemn sin in the flesh?
options: He allowed Jesus to be crucified
Repentance was made possible for the forgiveness of sin
Resurrection of the flesh rendered sin ineffective
He sent His own Son in the likeness of man
explanation: Romans 8:3: 'God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh.'
proTip: Learn Romans 8:3: God's action was sending His own Son.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: 'But you are not in darkness, brethren, for that day to surprise you like a thief.' That 'day' refers to the
explanation: 1 Thessalonians 5:2 calls it 'the day of the Lord' that comes like a thief in the night, referring to the second coming of Christ.
proTip: 'The Day of the Lord' = Christ's second coming.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: The main aim of the teaching of Christ's humility in Paul's Letter to the Philippians is that every Christian should
options: regard himself as equal to Jesus because He came in human form
confess that Jesus Christ is LORD to the glory of God the Father
work out his own salvation with fear and trembling
look into the interest of others and do nothing from selfishness
explanation: Paul introduces Christ's example by urging 'Do nothing from selfishness or conceit... look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others' (Philippians 2:3-4). Christ's humility is the model.
proTip: Humility in Philippians 2: Christ's self-emptying as a pattern for selfless service.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to Paul's Letter to the Philippians, God exalted Jesus and gave Him a name which is above all names because He
options: was humble and obedient unto death
was the greatest man ever born
explanation: Philippians 2:8-9: 'he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him.'
proTip: Humility leads to exaltation: the 'therefore' in verse 9 gives the reason.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: In the Letter to the Galatians, Christians are encouraged to bear one another's burdens in order to
explanation: Galatians 6:2: 'Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.'
proTip: The 'law of Christ' is the law of love shown in practical help.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: 'Be angry but do not sin' means that anger
options: is not a sin at all
could be an occasion for sin
explanation: Ephesians 4:26-27 warns, 'Be angry but do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil.' Anger itself is not always sin, but it can easily lead to it if held on to.
proTip: Control anger and settle it quickly so it does not become an opportunity for sin.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: There are varieties of gifts and so different people have different gifts. Who gives all these gifts?
explanation: 1 Corinthians 12:4 says there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; verse 11 says one and the same Spirit apportions them to each one as He wills.
proTip: All spiritual gifts come from the one Holy Spirit.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: The overriding principle in the use of spiritual gifts is
explanation: After regulating tongues and prophecy, Paul concludes, 'all things should be done decently and in order' (1 Corinthians 14:40). Gifts are to be exercised for the building up of the church. (Note: 1 Corinthians 13 also places love above all gifts, so check this item against your answer key.)
proTip: 1 Corinthians 14: gifts are for edification, exercised with decency and order.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: For the administration of the churches, Paul directed that Christians should
options: surrender all they have to the church
explanation: 1 Corinthians 16:2: 'On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper.' Giving is to be regular and proportionate.
proTip: Paul's giving principles: regular, proportionate, planned.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Contribution of relief materials for the needy in the church, according to Paul, must be
explanation: 2 Corinthians 9:7: 'Each one must do as he has made up his mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.'
proTip: Giving must be voluntary and cheerful, never forced.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Paul teaches that we should obey governing authorities in order to avoid
options: God's wrath and a bad conscience
explanation: Romans 13:5: 'Therefore one must be subject, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience.'
proTip: Obedience to authority: avoid wrath and keep a clear conscience.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: When Paul says 'if anyone will not work, let him not eat,' he is saying that
options: the lazy person must eat only a little
everyone should toil and labour with his hands
every person should seek a lucrative job
explanation: 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12 addresses idlers who lived off others. Paul commands them to work quietly and earn their own living, as he and his companions did with toil and labour (3:8).
proTip: Dignity of labour: Christians must work and not depend on others.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Paul worked harder than any of the apostles because
options: he had the strength to do so
of the grace of God that was with him
Jesus personally revealed Himself to him
he was formerly a persecutor of the church
explanation: 1 Corinthians 15:10: 'I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God which is with me.' Paul credits God's grace for his labour.
proTip: Paul credits his labour to God's grace, not to himself.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
subTopic: Christian living in the community - Colossians 3:18
question: Christian wives are to be subject to their husbands
options: since their husbands take care of them
because it is fitting in the LORD
because it is the natural thing to do
since women are not expected to be heard
explanation: Colossians 3:18: 'Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.' Verse 19 balances this by commanding husbands to love their wives.
proTip: Paul's household code: mutual duties grounded in the Lord.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: On being revealed at the coming of Christ, the lawless one will be slain by the
explanation: 2 Thessalonians 2:8: 'the lawless one will be revealed, and the Lord Jesus will slay him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by his appearing and his coming.'
proTip: The Lord destroys the lawless one effortlessly, by 'the breath of his mouth'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: An important feature of the second coming of Jesus as taught by Paul is the
options: establishment of a world government under Christ
explanation: 1 Thessalonians 4:16 says that at the Lord's descent 'the dead in Christ will rise first.' The resurrection of the dead is a key feature of Paul's teaching on the Parousia.
proTip: At the second coming, the dead in Christ rise first.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: 'What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.' This statement refers to the
options: good works which are expected of the Christian
reward of the works of Christians
explanation: In 1 Corinthians 15:36, Paul uses the seed image to answer 'How are the dead raised?' The seed dies and is raised in a new form, just as the body is raised imperishable.
proTip: Paul's seed analogy illustrates resurrection.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Paul's experience as recorded in his second Letter to the Corinthians teaches that the attitude of Christians to suffering should be that of
explanation: Paul lists beatings, imprisonments, shipwrecks and dangers (2 Corinthians 11), yet endures them, saying 'when I am weak, then I am strong' (12:10). The lesson is perseverance in suffering.
proTip: Paul's suffering teaches endurance, not retreat.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: In the Letter to the Hebrews, it is found that despite the victory through faith in God of the men of old, they did not receive what was promised. What was this promise?
explanation: Hebrews 11:39-40 says that though they were commended for their faith, they did not receive what was promised, since God had foreseen something better for us. The fulfilment of the promise is found in Christ.
proTip: Old Testament faith looked forward to the fulfilment of God's promise in Christ. Check against your answer key.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Abraham's faith and works were better illustrated when he
options: took Lot with him to Canaan
offered his son, Isaac, on the altar
explanation: James 2:21-22 cites Abraham offering Isaac on the altar as proof that 'faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by works.'
proTip: James's example for faith plus works: Abraham offering Isaac.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: 'Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for... For by it the men of old received divine approval.' Who are the men of old mentioned as examples of faith in the Letter to the Hebrews?
explanation: Hebrews 11 names Abel (v. 4), Abraham (v. 8) and Rahab (v. 31) among the heroes of faith. The other options include persons not listed there.
proTip: Hebrews 11 = the 'Hall of Faith': Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to James, effective prayer is that which is offered
explanation: James 1:6 says to ask 'in faith, with no doubting,' and 5:15 says 'the prayer of faith will save the sick man.' Effective prayer rests on faith, not volume or emotion.
proTip: Effective prayer = faith plus righteousness (James 5:16).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
subTopic: Christian living in the community - 1 Peter 2:12
question: According to Peter, Christians living among non-Christians should
explanation: 1 Peter 2:12: 'Maintain good conduct among the Gentiles, so that... they may see your good deeds and glorify God.' Christian witness is through good behaviour.
proTip: Peter's advice: let good conduct win outsiders.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Peter enjoins Christians to be good citizens by
options: using their freedom to fight for their right
explanation: 1 Peter 2:13: 'Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor... or to governors.' Christians are to honour all men and the emperor, and use freedom without making it a pretext for evil.
proTip: Both Paul (Romans 13) and Peter teach submission to civil authorities.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Sovereignty of God - creation of man (Genesis 1:26-27)
question: 'Let us make man in our image...' In the statement above, 'man' refers to
explanation: Genesis 1:26-27 says God made man in His image: 'male and female he created them.' 'Man' here means humankind, both male and female.
proTip: In Genesis 1:26-27 'man' = humankind, male and female together.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: In the covenant with Noah, God equates blood with
explanation: Genesis 9:4-6: God forbade eating flesh with its blood, 'for the life of the flesh is in the blood,' and declared that whoever sheds human blood shall have his own blood shed. Blood stands for life.
proTip: Blood = life in the Noahic covenant, so human life is sacred.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The covenant with Abraham stipulates that an uncircumcised male shall
options: find it difficult to have a child
be cut off from his people
explanation: Genesis 17:14: 'Any uncircumcised male... shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant.' Circumcision was the sign of the covenant.
proTip: Circumcision is the sign of the Abrahamic covenant; breaking it meant being cut off.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Joseph was hated the more by his brothers because
options: he was the first son of Rebecca
his father bought him a coat of many colours
explanation: Genesis 37:5 says that when Joseph told his dream, his brothers 'hated him yet more'; verse 8 repeats, 'they hated him yet more for his dreams and for his words.' The coat and his father's favour caused earlier hatred (37:3-4).
proTip: The words 'the more' point to the dreams, which added to the earlier hatred.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Pharaoh set Joseph over all the land of Egypt because he was
explanation: After Joseph interpreted the dreams and proposed a plan, Pharaoh said, 'there is none so discreet and wise as you are' (Genesis 41:39) and made him ruler over Egypt.
proTip: Pharaoh's own words: 'discreet and wise'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Divine Providence, Guidance and Protection - Moses and the burning bush (Exodus 3)
question: In the burning bush, God revealed Himself to Moses as the God of
explanation: In Exodus 3:6-10 God identified Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, saw the affliction of His people, and sent Moses to bring them out of Egypt. The revelation is of a God who delivers.
proTip: The burning bush reveals a God who sees, hears and delivers.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Divine Providence, Guidance and Protection - the Exodus (Exodus 13:17-18)
question: When the Hebrews left Egypt, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines because
options: He did not want them to see war and return to Egypt
He wanted to test their faith
the Hebrews went out of Egypt not equipped for war
explanation: Exodus 13:17: 'God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said, "Lest the people repent when they see war, and return to Egypt."'
proTip: The shorter route was avoided so the people would not lose heart and turn back.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Samuel's reaction during his first encounter with God showed that he was
options: afraid of the voice he heard
explanation: 1 Samuel 3:7 says Samuel 'did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.' He thrice mistook God's voice for Eli's until Eli guided him.
proTip: Samuel did not recognise God's voice because he was still inexperienced.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: From the accounts in the First Book of Samuel, Eli's attitude to his children showed parental
explanation: Eli only mildly rebuked Hophni and Phinehas for their sins; 1 Samuel 3:13 says God judged his house because 'his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them.'
proTip: Eli's failure to discipline his sons is the standard example of weak parental control.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: David - submission to the will of God (1 Samuel 24; 26)
question: David demonstrated his submission to the will of God when he
options: lamented the death of Saul and Jonathan
explanation: David twice refused to kill Saul, saying he would not stretch out his hand against 'the LORD's anointed' (1 Samuel 24:6; 26:9-11), leaving vengeance and the timing of kingship to God.
proTip: David's refusal to kill Saul is the key example of submission to God's will.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: When David repented of his adultery with Bathsheba, he said,
options: 'The man who has done this deserves to die...'
explanation: After Nathan's parable, David said, 'I have sinned against the LORD' (2 Samuel 12:13), and Nathan told him the LORD had put away his sin. 'The man who has done this deserves to die' (12:5) was David's reaction to the parable, before he realised it was about him.
proTip: 'I have sinned against the LORD' is David's confession; Psalm 51 opens with 'Have mercy on me'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Sovereignty of God - Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:12)
question: 'The Lord has set the sun in the heavens, but has said that he would dwell in thick darkness...' This was said at the
explanation: 1 Kings 8:12 records Solomon's words at the dedication of the Temple: 'The LORD has set the sun in the heavens, but has said that he would dwell in thick darkness,' after the cloud filled the house (8:10-11).
proTip: Solomon's dedication prayer (1 Kings 8) says God dwells in thick darkness, i.e. His presence is awesome and unseen.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: In the first three chapters of the Book of Hosea, his main teaching is that
options: God loves us despite our sins
one should keep the commandments of God
explanation: Hosea's marriage to the unfaithful Gomer is an image of God's steadfast love for unfaithful Israel; God still calls His people back (Hosea 2:14-23; 3:1-5).
proTip: Hosea 1-3: God's faithful love for Israel despite her unfaithfulness.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: The valley of Achor in the Book of Hosea is a door of
explanation: Hosea 2:15: 'I will make the Valley of Achor a door of hope.' Achor, a place of trouble (Joshua 7), becomes a place of hope under God's restoration.
proTip: Hosea 2:15: the Valley of Achor becomes 'a door of hope'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice, true religion and divine love - Hosea 6:1-3
question: 'Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn, that he may heal us; he has stricken, and he will bind us up.' This call is to encourage
options: response to the need of the nation
explanation: Hosea 6:1-3 is a call to return to the LORD, who both disciplines and heals. It is an invitation to respond to God's love, though verse 4 shows the people's love was fleeting. (Note: the source has no answer key, so check this item against yours.)
proTip: Hosea 6:1-3 invites a return to God; His love heals, but repentance must be sincere (6:6).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: With reference to prophet Isaiah's vision, which of the following attributes must a minister of God possess?
explanation: Isaiah saw the LORD thrice proclaimed 'Holy' and confessed his own uncleanness; his lips were cleansed before he was sent (Isaiah 6:1-8). A minister must be cleansed and holy.
proTip: Isaiah 6: God's holiness demands holiness in His minister.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: What did God give to Ezekiel to eat in his vision?
explanation: Ezekiel 2:9-3:3: God gave him a scroll to eat, which was 'as sweet as honey' in his mouth.
proTip: Ezekiel eats a scroll = he must absorb God's message before delivering it.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Baptism and Temptation of Jesus - Matthew 3:13-17
question: Jesus was baptized by John the Baptist
options: to fulfil the prophecy about Him
so that the heavens could open up blessings for all believers
so that the Holy Spirit could descend upon Him
explanation: When John hesitated, Jesus answered, 'it is fitting for us in this way to fulfil all righteousness' (Matthew 3:15). He identified with sinners and obeyed God's will.
proTip: Jesus' own reason in Matthew 3:15: 'to fulfil all righteousness'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Baptism and Temptation of Jesus - Matthew 3:17; Luke 3:22
question: 'Thou art my beloved Son; with thee I am well pleased.' This statement was made during the
explanation: Mark 1:11 and Luke 3:22 record this voice from heaven addressed to Jesus at His baptism. At the transfiguration the voice says 'This is my beloved Son' (Matthew 17:5).
proTip: Baptism: 'Thou art my beloved Son'. Transfiguration: 'This is my beloved Son'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Baptism and Temptation of Jesus - Matthew 4:1-11; Luke 4:1-13
question: According to the temptation narratives in the gospels according to Matthew and Luke, Jesus overcame Satan because He
options: depended on the word of God
explanation: Each time Satan tempted Him, Jesus replied 'It is written...' quoting Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10).
proTip: Jesus defeated temptation by citing Scripture: 'It is written'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: 'Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?' On what occasion was this question asked?
options: When Jesus ate in the house of Zacchaeus
Following the invitation of Jesus to a meal by a Pharisee
explanation: After Jesus called Matthew, He ate in his house with many tax collectors and sinners, and the Pharisees asked this question (Matthew 9:9-11). Jesus replied that He came to call sinners, not the righteous.
proTip: The Pharisees' complaint follows the call of Matthew, a tax collector.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Discipleship - the cost of following Jesus (Matthew 8:21-22)
question: 'Follow me and leave the dead to bury their own dead.' By this statement, Jesus means that
options: there is no life after death
following Him comes before anything else
disciples should leave their families in God's care
explanation: A would-be disciple wanted to bury his father first; Jesus' reply shows that discipleship takes priority over every other duty (Matthew 8:21-22; Luke 9:59-60).
proTip: Jesus' call takes first place above family duties.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The disciples became terrified when they saw Jesus walking on the sea because
options: they thought He was a ghost
there was a great storm in the sea
explanation: Mark 6:49 says that when they saw him walking on the sea 'they thought it was a ghost, and cried out.' Jesus calmed them: 'Take heart, it is I; have no fear.'
proTip: The disciples mistook Jesus for a ghost.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: By the miracle of raising Lazarus to life, Jesus wanted to
options: reward Mary and Martha for their charity
convince the people that He was the LORD of life
explanation: Jesus said, 'I am the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25) and prayed aloud 'that they may believe that thou didst send me' (11:42). The miracle showed His authority over death.
proTip: Lazarus' raising is a sign that Jesus is the resurrection and the life.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Miracles - healing at the pool of Bethzatha (John 5:1-18)
question: The Jews sought all the more to kill Jesus after the healing of the man at the pool of Bethzatha because they thought that He
options: claimed to have authority to forgive sins
did not agree with the law of Moses
said that He was born before Abraham
explanation: John 5:18: 'the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the sabbath but also called God his Father, making himself equal with God.'
proTip: John 5:18 gives the reason: He called God His Father, making Himself equal with God.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: In the gospel according to Matthew, the disciples could not heal the epileptic boy because
options: the boy's father had no faith in them
explanation: Jesus told the disciples, 'Because of your little faith' (Matthew 17:20). (Mark 9:29 adds prayer, but the question asks for Matthew.)
proTip: Match the gospel: Matthew says 'little faith'; Mark adds prayer.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: In the parable of the sower, the seed which fell on rocky ground refers to people whose conversion is
explanation: Mark 4:16-17: such people receive the word with joy but have no root, endure only for a while, and fall away at tribulation. Their conversion is shallow.
proTip: Rocky ground = shallow, short-lived faith.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The parable of the lost sheep teaches much about God's
explanation: The shepherd leaves ninety-nine to seek one lost sheep and rejoices when it is found, showing God's love and concern for each sinner (Luke 15:3-7).
proTip: The lost sheep, coin and son show God's love for sinners.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Turning the other cheek as preached by Jesus implies that believers should
explanation: Matthew 5:39: 'do not resist one who is evil. But if any one strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.' The teaching replaces retaliation with non-resistance.
proTip: 'Turn the other cheek' = do not retaliate.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Matthew's account of the gospel, Jesus charged the twelve disciples to give without pay because they themselves
explanation: Matthew 10:8: 'You received without pay, give without pay.'
proTip: Freely received, freely give.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Which disciples were with Jesus during the transfiguration?
explanation: Matthew 17:1: 'Jesus took with him Peter and James and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain.'
proTip: The inner circle: Peter, James and John.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing - Luke 19:41-44
question: Jesus wept over Jerusalem because
options: the people did not believe in Him
the city did not know the things that made for peace
people were buying and selling in the temple
the Pharisees and the priests had misled the people
explanation: Luke 19:41-42: 'And when he drew near and saw the city he wept over it, saying, "Would that even today you knew the things that make for peace!"'
proTip: Jesus wept because Jerusalem did not recognise the things that made for peace.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing - Luke 19:37-38
question: In the Gospel according to Luke, the multitude that followed Jesus during the triumphal entry rejoiced and praised God with a loud voice because
options: they realized that Jesus was a prophet from Nazareth
of the mighty works that they had seen done by Jesus
Jesus was for the first time riding on a colt
they believed that Jesus would deliver them from the hands of their enemies
explanation: Luke 19:37: the whole multitude of the disciples 'began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen.' (The 'prophet from Nazareth' remark is in Matthew 21:11.)
proTip: Luke gives the mighty works as the reason; Matthew mentions the prophet from Nazareth.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Trials and Death of Jesus - Matthew 26:51-54
question: Jesus did not appeal to His Father for legions of angels to fight for Him because
options: it was not proper for angels to physically fight human beings
He could, on His own, avoid the cross
He wanted the scriptures to be fulfilled
the disciples were watching and praying
explanation: In Matthew 26:53-54 Jesus said He could ask for more than twelve legions of angels, 'But how then should the scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?'
proTip: Jesus willingly went to the cross to fulfil the scriptures.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Trials and Death of Jesus - Luke 23:6-12
question: What did Pilate achieve by sending Jesus to Herod?
options: He escaped the anger of the Jews
Jesus was not killed in his hands
He was able to pacify the Jews
explanation: Luke 23:12: 'And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.'
proTip: Luke 23:12 records the unintended result: Herod and Pilate became friends.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Trials and Death of Jesus - Mark 15:33-36
question: Which of Jesus' words on the cross led a bystander to give him vinegar?
options: 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.'
'Father, into thy hands I commit my spirit.'
'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'
explanation: In Mark 15:34-36, after Jesus cried 'Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?' bystanders thought He was calling Elijah, and one ran and filled a sponge with vinegar. (In John 19:28-29 the vinegar follows 'I thirst', which is not among the options.)
proTip: The cry of dereliction led to the vinegar in Mark and Matthew.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Teachings about Himself - Resurrection and Life (John 11:21-27)
question: When Jesus said that Lazarus would rise again, Martha thought that
options: Jesus would raise her brother from the dead
her brother would rise again at the last day
Jesus was talking of His own resurrection
He was talking of spiritual resurrection
explanation: Martha answered, 'I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day' (John 11:24). Jesus then declared, 'I am the resurrection and the life.'
proTip: Martha expected a future resurrection; Jesus pointed to Himself as the resurrection.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Fellowship in the Early Church - Acts 1:21-26
question: What kind of a man was elected to replace Judas Iscariot?
options: An opponent of the religious leaders
explanation: Acts 1:21-22: the replacement had to be a man who accompanied them throughout Jesus' ministry, 'one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.' Matthias was chosen.
proTip: Qualification for the replacement apostle: a companion and a witness to the resurrection.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The event of the day of Pentecost was prophesied by
explanation: In Acts 2:16-21 Peter explains the event: 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel', quoting Joel 2:28-32.
proTip: Pentecost = Joel 2:28-32 fulfilled.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Who was the second martyr of the early church?
explanation: Stephen was the first martyr (Acts 7). In Acts 12:2 Herod killed James the brother of John with the sword, the second martyr.
proTip: Stephen is first (Acts 7); James, John's brother, is second (Acts 12:2).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: The Christian concept of justification is that
options: through faith in Jesus the sinner is now regarded by God as guiltless
by one's efforts in keeping the law, man is now perfect before God
through his own knowledge, man can now do what is pleasing to God
by his natural wisdom, a sinner could be reconciled to God
explanation: Romans 3:24-26 says believers are 'justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus.' Justification is God's declaration of the believer as righteous through faith.
proTip: Justification = God's gracious declaration of righteousness through faith in Christ.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to Paul, those who rely on the works of the law are under a curse since
options: the law is made for the weak
none can fully keep the law
the works of the law are of the devil
explanation: Galatians 3:10 quotes Deuteronomy 27:26: 'Cursed be every one who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law.' Since no one keeps it perfectly, reliance on it brings a curse.
proTip: The law demands perfect obedience, which no one gives; hence faith in Christ.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to the Letter of Paul to the Romans, sin reigned in death, while grace reigned through righteousness to
explanation: Romans 5:21: 'as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.'
proTip: Learn the verse: grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Christians believe that they are children of God because
options: they keep the laws and covenants of Abraham as commanded by God
they are church goers and benefactors
they are descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
through faith, they were baptized into Christ and put on Christ
explanation: Galatians 3:26-27: 'in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.'
proTip: Sonship comes through faith and baptism into Christ, not descent or law-keeping.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Christians ought to be humble because
options: only the humble will inherit eternal life
explanation: Philippians 2:5-8: 'Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus... he humbled himself and became obedient unto death.' Christ is the model of humility.
proTip: Christian humility is rooted in Christ's example.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to Paul, spiritual gifts, if properly employed, help in
explanation: 1 Corinthians 14:12: 'strive to excel in building up the church'; verse 26: 'Let all things be done for edification.' Gifts are for the common good (12:7).
proTip: Spiritual gifts are for edifying (building up) the church.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Paul advised Christians in Thessalonica to keep away from any brother who is
explanation: 2 Thessalonians 3:6: 'keep away from any brother who is living in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.' Idlers were to work and earn their living.
proTip: Idleness in Thessalonica: Paul says to work quietly and not be dependent.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: The order of events at the second coming of Christ will be that
options: those who are alive will be caught up first before the dead will rise
the dead will rise first before the living are caught up
the dead and the living will be caught up together
only the dead will rise leaving behind those who are alive
explanation: 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17: 'we who are alive... shall not precede those who have fallen asleep... the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive... shall be caught up together with them.'
proTip: The dead in Christ rise first, then the living are caught up.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Which of the following commandments is described by James as the royal law?
options: You shall have no other gods before me
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart
You shall love your neighbour as yourself
You shall not covet your neighbour's property
explanation: James 2:8: 'If you really fulfil the royal law, according to the scripture, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself," you do well.' James uses it to condemn favouritism.
proTip: The royal law = love your neighbour as yourself (James 2:8).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
subTopic: Christian living in the community - Romans 12:20
question: 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him...' This statement implies
explanation: Romans 12:20-21: 'if your enemy is hungry, feed him... Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.' Paul teaches kindness to enemies instead of revenge.
proTip: Return kindness for evil; do not seek vengeance.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: In extolling the sovereignty of God, Amos contrasted Him with the Nile, which he described as
options: the source of the waters of the sea
explanation: Amos 9:5 says the land of the LORD 'rises like the Nile, and sinks again, like the Nile of Egypt'; 8:8 uses the same image. God controls the earth, while the Nile merely rises and sinks.
proTip: Amos 8:8 and 9:5 compare the rise and fall of the Nile to God's power over the earth.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: By keeping God's covenant, the people of Israel would become
options: a kingdom of priests to God
a nation where God would manifest Himself
explanation: Exodus 19:5-6: 'if you will obey my voice and keep my covenant... you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.'
proTip: Sinai covenant promise: a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Punishment and Hope - the New Covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34)
question: According to Jeremiah, the vital element in the new covenant God would make with the Jews was that
options: He would bless all nations through the Jews
man would be enabled to keep God's law
salvation would come through a virgin's seed
the individual would be accountable before God
explanation: Jeremiah 31:33: 'I will put my law within them, and I will write it upon their hearts.' The new covenant is internal: God's law written on the heart so that people can keep it. (Option D reflects Jeremiah 31:29-30, which accompanies it; check against your key.)
proTip: New covenant: the law moves from stone tablets to the heart.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Joseph saw his rise to a leadership position in Egypt in relation to his brothers as
options: a proof of his superiority over them
an opportunity to avenge their evil deeds
a time to test their honesty
a means of preserving their lives
explanation: Joseph told his brothers, 'God sent me before you to preserve life' (Genesis 45:5), and later, 'you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good... to save much people alive' (50:20).
proTip: Joseph interprets his rise as God's plan to preserve life.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: 'If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.' In the statement above, 'you' refers to
explanation: In Judges 4:8 Barak says this to Deborah when she told him to lead the army against Sisera. She agreed to go but said the honour would go to a woman.
proTip: Barak demanded Deborah's presence before he would go to battle.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The name Ichabod means
explanation: Phinehas' wife named her son Ichabod, saying, 'The glory has departed from Israel' (1 Samuel 4:21-22), after the ark was captured and Eli and his sons died. The name means 'no glory', so 'without glory' fits best, though 'departed glory' is a close alternative.
proTip: Ichabod = no glory; the glory had departed from Israel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: David - the death of his child (2 Samuel 12:15-23)
question: How did David perceive that his child from Bathsheba was dead?
options: Bathsheba lamented the loss of her child
He saw his servants whispering together
He received a message to that effect from Joab
God revealed it to him through Nathan
explanation: 2 Samuel 12:19: 'David saw that his servants were whispering together, and David understood that the child was dead.'
proTip: David inferred the death of his child from the whispering of his servants.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: 'As one falls before the wicked you have fallen.' This is part of David's lamentation over
explanation: 2 Samuel 3:33-34: David lamented, 'Should Abner die as a fool dies?... as one falls before the wicked you have fallen.' Abner had been treacherously killed by Joab.
proTip: David's laments: Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 1), Abner (2 Sam 3), Absalom (2 Sam 18).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: The mother of the living child asked Solomon to give the child to the other woman because
options: killing the child would serve no useful purpose
her heart yearned for the child
she was confident that the king would ensure justice
she believed the child would recognize her at maturity
explanation: 1 Kings 3:26: 'her heart yearned for her son, and she said, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means slay it."' Her compassion revealed her as the true mother.
proTip: Solomon's wisdom exposed the true mother by her compassion.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice, true religion and divine love - Hosea 1-3
question: Hosea's matrimonial experience symbolizes God's intention to
options: reform Israel and make her greater
explanation: God told Hosea to love an adulterous woman 'as the LORD loves the people of Israel' (Hosea 3:1); Hosea bought Gomer back (3:2-3). The marriage shows God's intention to redeem Israel despite her unfaithfulness.
proTip: Hosea's marriage = God's redeeming love for unfaithful Israel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice, true religion and divine love - Hosea 1:2
question: The harlotry of Gomer is compared to Israel's
explanation: Hosea 1:2: 'the land commits great harlotry by forsaking the LORD.' Gomer's infidelity pictures Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness.
proTip: Gomer = Israel; harlotry = unfaithfulness to God.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.' This was said in the year that
options: David brought the ark to Jerusalem
explanation: Isaiah 6:1: 'In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne,' and the seraphim cried this in verse 3.
proTip: Isaiah's call came in the year King Uzziah died.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
subTopic: Social justice and true religion - Isaiah 1:10
question: 'Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah!' The nation referred to as Sodom and Gomorrah in this statement is
explanation: Isaiah 1:1 says his vision concerned Judah and Jerusalem, and verses 9-10 compare Judah's rulers and people to Sodom and Gomorrah because of their corruption.
proTip: Isaiah's primary audience was Judah and Jerusalem.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
question: Jeremiah was not anxious to accept God's call to become a prophet because
options: he knew that people would not listen to him
he needed to know God more
he was too young and inexperienced
explanation: Jeremiah 1:6: 'Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth.' God told him not to say he was only a youth.
proTip: Jeremiah's objection: 'I am only a youth'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Baptism and Temptation of Jesus - Matthew 4:1-11
question: The devil's principal purpose for tempting Jesus Christ was to
options: show that nobody is above temptation
demonstrate that he controls the world
lure Jesus Christ from his mission
prove that after all, Jesus is only human
explanation: Each temptation (bread, the temple pinnacle, the kingdoms of the world) offered an easier way than obedient suffering as Messiah, trying to turn Jesus from His mission (Matthew 4:3-10).
proTip: The temptations aimed at drawing Jesus away from His mission.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head.' The statement above implies that
options: the Son of man needs no house
explanation: Jesus said this to a man who promised to follow Him anywhere (Luke 9:57-58). It warns that discipleship involves sacrifice and giving up comfort.
proTip: Luke 9:57-62 is about the cost of discipleship.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Luke, following Jesus involves
explanation: Luke 9:23: 'If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.'
proTip: Luke 9:23: deny yourself, take up your cross daily, follow Jesus.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Miracles - the healing ministry of Jesus
question: In the healing ministry of Jesus Christ, which of the following played a very vital role?
explanation: Jesus often said 'Your faith has made you well' (Mark 5:34; 10:52; Luke 17:19) and at Nazareth could do few mighty works because of unbelief (Mark 6:5-6).
proTip: Faith is the usual condition in Jesus' healing miracles.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Miracles - the widow's son at Nain (Luke 7:11-17)
question: Jesus healed the only son of the widow of Nain because
options: the widow demonstrated faith in Him
He wanted to make people believe in Him
explanation: Luke 7:13: 'when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, "Do not weep."' She had not asked for help.
proTip: Nain: raised purely out of Jesus' compassion; no one asked.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The healing of the paralytic brought by his four friends demonstrates
options: the power of Jesus to heal all types of diseases
that the friends had faith in the healing power of Jesus
the compassion of Jesus on the sick man
that Jesus has power to forgive sin
explanation: Jesus said, 'that you may know that the Son of man has authority on earth to forgive sins' - and then healed the man (Mark 2:10-11). The healing authenticated His power to forgive sin.
proTip: Mark 2:10: the healing proves His authority to forgive sins.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Mark and Luke, the response of blind Bartimaeus to healing was to
options: run to show himself to the priests
speak to the Jews about Jesus
explanation: Mark 10:52: 'immediately he received his sight and followed him on the way'; Luke 18:43 adds that he followed Jesus glorifying God.
proTip: Bartimaeus followed Jesus; the leper cases involve showing oneself to the priests.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The parable which teaches about God's judgment is that of the
explanation: In the parable of the weeds (tares) the weeds are gathered and burned at the harvest, which Jesus explains as the final judgment (Matthew 13:40-43).
proTip: Weeds = final separation and judgment at the end of the age.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: The parable of the Good Samaritan implies that
options: priests and Levites hardly show love
neighbourliness is expressed in love and concern
a good neighbour must show love to his enemies
explanation: Jesus asked, 'Which of these three... proved neighbour to the man?' and the lawyer answered 'The one who showed mercy'; Jesus said, 'Go and do likewise' (Luke 10:36-37).
proTip: A neighbour is the one who shows mercy to anyone in need.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Luke ends the sermon on the plain with an analogy of a building to emphasize the importance of
options: preaching and abiding by the word
explanation: The two houses (Luke 6:47-49) illustrate the one who hears Jesus' words and does them, versus the one who hears and does not.
proTip: Wise builder = hears and does the word.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus implies in His teaching on adultery, prayer, alms and fasting that these are more matters of
explanation: Jesus taught that adultery begins in the heart (Matthew 5:28) and that alms, prayer and fasting must not be for show but for God who sees in secret (6:1-18).
proTip: Sermon on the Mount stresses inner motives, not outward display.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: Jesus' injunction not to lay up treasure on earth for ourselves implies that the Christian should
explanation: Jesus teaches that treasures in heaven are the lasting ones (Matthew 6:19-21). In the same spirit, Luke 12:21 speaks of being rich toward God, and 1 Timothy 6:18 of being rich in good deeds.
proTip: Heavenly treasure means lasting spiritual values, not literally refusing to bank money.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Mission of the Disciples - the Seventy (Luke 10:17-20)
question: The seventy disciples who returned from their missionary work were told by Jesus to rejoice because
options: they were well received by people
the spirits were subject to them
their names were written in heaven
explanation: Luke 10:20: 'do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
proTip: Rejoice in salvation, not in spiritual power.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Matthew, when Jesus was transfigured
options: His face shone like the sun
His body became as white as light
He could only communicate with heaven
explanation: Matthew 17:2: 'his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as light.' Moses and Elijah, not Elisha, appeared.
proTip: Matthew 17:2: face shone like the sun; garments white as light.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing - Matthew 21:1-7
question: According to Matthew, Jesus entered Jerusalem riding
explanation: Matthew 21:2-7 (RSV): the disciples brought 'the ass and the colt', fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. Matthew alone mentions both animals.
proTip: Matthew mentions both the ass and the colt; Mark and Luke mention only the colt.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Trials and Death of Jesus - Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36-44)
question: The prayer of Jesus before his arrest showed that
options: His disciples had not understood Him thoroughly
He was not prepared to die on the cross
He wanted His disciples to be prayerful
explanation: Matthew 26:37-38: Jesus 'began to be sorrowful and troubled' and said, 'My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.' He still submitted: 'not as I will, but as thou wilt' (26:39).
proTip: Gethsemane shows Jesus' real distress and total submission to the Father.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Trials and Death of Jesus - Matthew 27:11-14
question: 'Are you the King of the Jews?' Jesus' reply to this question by Pilate was
options: 'My kingship is not of this world'
'Who made me a judge or divider over you?'
'Why put me to the test, you hypocrites?'
explanation: Matthew 27:11: Pilate asked, 'Are you the King of the Jews?' Jesus said, 'You have said so.' 'My kingship is not of this world' is from John 18:36.
proTip: Match the gospel: Matthew's reply is 'You have said so'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: According to Matthew, when the women went to see the sepulchre, they
options: found that the disciples had been there
saw an angel sitting upon the stone
found the guards rolling back the stone
explanation: Matthew 28:2: an angel of the Lord descended, rolled back the stone and sat upon it. The angel told the women Jesus had risen (28:5-6).
proTip: Matthew: an angel sat on the rolled-back stone.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Teachings about Himself - the True Vine (John 15:1-8)
question: Jesus used the illustration of the vine to teach that a Christian that abides in Him will surely
explanation: John 15:5: 'He who abides in me, and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.'
proTip: Abide in Christ and you bear fruit.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Fellowship in the Early Church - the seven (Acts 6:1-6)
question: Two of the seven men chosen to serve tables in the early church were
explanation: Acts 6:5 lists Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus. Only option A names two of the seven.
proTip: The seven: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, Nicolaus.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Holy Spirit and Mission - Simon the magician (Acts 8:18-24)
question: 'Give me also this power, that any one on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.' The man who made this request was
explanation: Simon offered the apostles money for this power, and Peter said, 'Your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money' (Acts 8:18-20). (The source stem was cut off; I reconstructed it from the options, so check it against your copy.)
proTip: Simon the magician thought the Spirit could be bought, hence 'simony'.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
question: At the Beautiful Gate, Peter and John healed a man who was
explanation: Acts 3:2 describes a man lame from birth who was carried daily to the Beautiful Gate; Peter said, 'In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk' (3:6).
proTip: The Beautiful Gate: a man lame from birth.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION C: Themes from the four Gospels and Acts of the Apostles
subTopic: Mission to the Gentiles - Jerusalem Council (Galatians 2:9)
question: The people referred to as pillars of the Jerusalem church, who gave Barnabas and Paul the right hand of fellowship, were
explanation: Galatians 2:9: 'James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.'
proTip: Pillars of the Jerusalem church: James, Cephas (Peter) and John.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: The condition for justification according to Paul is
explanation: Romans 3:28: 'a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law.' Galatians 2:16 adds faith in Jesus Christ.
proTip: Justification is by faith in Christ, not by merit or law.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: On which of the following grounds will faith be null and the promise void?
options: Faith is a necessary condition for justification
Salvation comes through adherence to the law
explanation: Romans 4:14: 'if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.' The promise depends on faith so that it may rest on grace.
proTip: If the law brings the inheritance, faith and promise are meaningless.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to the Letter of Paul to the Romans, Christians are to yield themselves to God as men who
options: have been raised from death to life
no longer live by the works of law
have listened to the gospel of Christ
explanation: Romans 6:13: 'yield yourselves to God as men who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments of righteousness.'
proTip: Romans 6:13: yield yourselves to God as those brought from death to life.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, into the world in the likeness of sinful flesh in order
options: that the law might be fulfilled
that man may walk in the flesh
explanation: Romans 8:3-4: God sent His Son 'in order that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.'
proTip: Christ came to fulfil the law's requirement in us.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: '...at the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord...' The statement above demonstrates the Lordship of Jesus over
explanation: Philippians 2:10 extends the Lordship of Jesus 'in heaven and on earth and under the earth' - all creation.
proTip: Philippians 2:10-11: universal Lordship of Christ.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Paul told the Corinthians that if anyone has caused pain to the church, he should be
explanation: 2 Corinthians 2:7: 'you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.'
proTip: Church discipline should end in forgiveness and comfort.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: The greatest spiritual gift to seek is
explanation: 1 Corinthians 12:31 points to 'a still more excellent way', and chapter 13 ends: 'the greatest of these is love' (13:13).
proTip: 1 Corinthians 13: love is the greatest gift.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: One of the civic responsibilities Christians are commanded to carry out is
explanation: Romans 13:1: 'Let every person be subject to the governing authorities.' Verses 6-7 add paying taxes and giving respect.
proTip: Paul and Peter: obey lawful civil authorities.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: In the course of his ministry, Paul worked night and day so that
options: he might not be a burden to anyone
he could raise money for the work of the gospel
he could pay the debt he was owing the brethren
explanation: 2 Thessalonians 3:8: 'we worked night and day, that we might not burden any of you.' Paul gave an example of self-support.
proTip: Paul worked with his hands so as not to be a burden.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: Those who have fallen asleep before the coming of the Lord are those who are
explanation: In 1 Thessalonians 4:13-15 'those who are asleep' are believers who have died. 'Sleep' is used as a gentle word for physical death.
proTip: 'Fallen asleep' = died physically.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: James enjoins Christians to remain impartial by
options: showing love to all without distinction
explanation: James 2:8-9: 'If you really fulfil the royal law... "You shall love your neighbour as yourself"... But if you show partiality, you commit sin.' (The options overlap in meaning; check against your key.)
proTip: James ties impartiality to the royal law of neighbourly love.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
question: According to James, the man who prays to God and at the same time doubts is
explanation: James 1:6-8: the one who doubts is 'like a wave of the sea driven and tossed by the wind... a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.'
proTip: Prayer must be offered in faith without doubting.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION D: Themes from Selected Epistles
subTopic: Christian living in the community - suffering (1 Peter 4:12-19)
question: Peter admonishes Christians that suffering for Christ's sake brings God's
explanation: 1 Peter 4:14: 'If you are reproached for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.'
proTip: 1 Peter 4:14: suffering for Christ = blessing.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: God made two great lights to
options: rule the day and the night
demarcate between the day and the night
explanation: Genesis 1:16 says God made 'the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night.' Verse 18 repeats that they were 'to rule over the day and over the night.'
proTip: On the fourth day the sun and moon were set to rule day and night.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: God commanded the earth to bring forth living creatures according to their kinds on the
explanation: Genesis 1:24-31: on the sixth day God made the cattle, creeping things and beasts of the earth, and then man. The fifth day was for sea creatures and birds (1:20-23).
proTip: Creation order: 5th day = sea creatures and birds; 6th day = land animals and man.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: When God heard the groaning of the people of Israel in Egypt, He
options: sent a warning to the Pharaoh
explanation: Exodus 2:24: 'God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.' The deliverance began from that.
proTip: God acts for Israel because of His covenant with the patriarchs.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Obedience and Disobedience - the golden calf (Exodus 32:1-6)
question: The golden calf which Aaron made for Israel was an evidence of
options: an attempt to revolt against God
explanation: When Moses delayed on the mountain, the people said, 'Make us gods who shall go before us' (Exodus 32:1), turning to an idol instead of trusting the God who had delivered them. (Their remark about Moses also shows impatience, so check against your key.)
proTip: The golden calf shows impatience and lack of faith in God.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Divine Providence, Guidance and Protection - Exodus 14:10-12
question: 'Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness?' This question was asked by the Israelites when
options: they were hungry in the wilderness
there was no water for them to drink
the spies brought evil reports about Canaan
explanation: Exodus 14:10-11: when the Israelites saw Pharaoh's army marching after them at the Red Sea, they cried out to the LORD and said this to Moses.
proTip: The graves-in-Egypt complaint was at the Red Sea, when the Egyptians pursued them.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: Divine Providence, Guidance and Protection - manna (Exodus 16:4)
question: God promised to send bread from heaven to the people of Israel, so as to see if they would
explanation: Exodus 16:4: 'Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you... that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law or not.'
proTip: Manna was a test of obedience to God's law.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: 'Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel, at which the two ears of everyone that hears it will tingle.' To whom did God speak these words?
explanation: 1 Samuel 3:11: 'Then the LORD said to Samuel, "Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel, at which the two ears of every one who hears it will tingle."' It announced judgment on Eli's house. (The source stem was cut off, so I reconstructed the question from the options.)
proTip: God spoke the judgment on Eli's house to the boy Samuel.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Why did David spare the life of King Saul at Ziph?
options: He did not want to shed blood
explanation: 1 Samuel 26:9: 'Do not destroy him; for who can put forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless?'
proTip: David respected Saul as the LORD's anointed.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
question: Nathan told David that although God had put away his sin, he would still be
explanation: 2 Samuel 12:13-14: 'The LORD has put away your sin... However, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child that is born to you shall die.'
proTip: Forgiveness does not always remove the consequences of sin.

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION A: Themes from Creation to the Division of the Kingdom
subTopic: The Sovereignty of God - Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:1-9)
question: The ark of the covenant brought before Israel and King Solomon contained
explanation: 1 Kings 8:9: 'There was nothing in the ark except the two tables of stone which Moses put there at Horeb.'
proTip: The ark held only the two tables of stone (1 Kings 8:9).

subject: Christian Religious Studies
topic: SECTION B: Themes from the Division of the Kingdom to the Return from Exile and the Prophets
